Direct Sample-Average Learning for Queueing Control:
Gradient-Free Top-KK Coarse-to-Fine Optimization

Mehrdad Nozohour Yazdi    Yiqiang Q. Zhao Affiliation: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Carleton University Email: mehrdadnozohouryazdi@cmail.carleton.ca    zhao@math.carleton.ca
October 18, 2026
Abstract

We study steady-state queueing control when decisions must be learned from a single persistent operating trajectory: only the implemented action produces data, and the queue is not reset when the action changes. Fixed-event-count cycles provide a direct ratio-of-totals sample-average approximation (SAA) of each action’s steady-state cost rate. A Top-KK coarse-to-fine (CTF) search then ranks these estimates, retains several promising refinement paths, and concentrates later operation on finer candidate sets. The method requires no gradient, convexity, or differentiability.

We decompose direct-SAA error into accumulated conditional transient bias and martingale fluctuation. For regenerative queues, a bias-function representation reduces transient effects within contiguous action blocks to boundary terms. A finite-sample triangular-array bound with Lyapunov-weighted innovation variance then links stagewise estimation accuracy to master-grid identification through guardian retention. The queueing and sampling hypotheses are verified completely for a specified persistent-workload M/M/1M/M/1 implementation. At a common active set, Top-KK has a weakly larger guardian margin than Top-1, and the implemented hierarchy supplies an exact-objective example in which Top-1 irreversibly discards the optimal refinement branch. This structural comparison does not assert uniform superiority of complete algorithms at equal budgets.

The numerical study delineates scope rather than universal dominance. With exact workload observations, Top-KK gives smaller terminal gaps than the corrected LiQUAR comparator in the reported samples, whereas LiQUAR has lower median cumulative learning cost at the large budget. Top-KK also improves on Top-1 and flat SAA in every budget of a new canonical, approximately clock-matched mixed discrete–continuous staffing experiment. A nonpreemptive lognormal-service experiment requires much longer horizons, while GOLiQ is markedly stronger on a smooth pricing–staffing benchmark designed for queueing sensitivities. Direct ranking is therefore best viewed as a complement when reliable model-specific gradients are unavailable, inconvenient, or mismatched to the operational decision space.

Keywords: queueing control; online learning; sample average approximation; coarse-to-fine optimization; gradient-free optimization; transient bias; mixed discrete–continuous control; heavy-tailed service.

1 Introduction

Many queueing-control problems require decisions to be made while the system is operating and while important model primitives are only partially known. A service provider may choose a price, staffing level, service capacity, routing rule, or admission threshold while learning from the same queueing trajectory generated by those decisions. The long-run target is a steady-state cost rate, but the observations immediately after a policy change are generally neither independent nor stationary: they inherit the congestion created by previous controls.

Two difficulties are coupled in this setting. First, objective values must be learned from dependent, inherited-state observations rather than from fresh steady-state samples. Second, a fine action grid may be too large to evaluate uniformly, so the learner must decide which regions deserve further operating time. The question addressed here is whether direct cost observations can support both statistically valid steady-state estimation and an economical multiresolution search without resetting the queue.

We study a route based on direct objective learning. For an action aa, let f⁡(a)f(a) denote its steady-state expected cost rate. We organize operation into cycles containing a fixed number DD of designated events and estimate f⁡(a)f(a) from the cumulative realized cost and cumulative clock time observed whenever aa is actually implemented:

f^n​(a)=cumulative realized cost under ​acumulative operating time under ​a.\widehat{f}_{n}(a)=\frac{\text{cumulative realized cost under }a}{\text{cumulative operating time under }a}.

No gradient or counterfactual trajectory is constructed. When realized cost is observable, the learner need not be supplied with a steady-state formula, a demand curve, or a service-time distribution.

A prominent alternative in online queueing optimization is to estimate or exploit gradients. Chen, Liu, and Hong [1] develop GOLiQ for joint pricing and capacity sizing, using queueing sensitivity information to form a stochastic gradient. Chen, Hong, and Liu [2] develop LiQUAR, which uses two perturbed controls to construct a finite-difference gradient when the demand function and service distribution are unknown. Queueing bandit methods provide another important route; see, among others, [4, 3]. These methods can be highly effective when their gradient, confidence, or regret structure fits the model. Our aim is not to replace them, but to develop the complementary case in which direct objective values are observable while reliable model-specific sensitivity information is unavailable, inconvenient, or poorly matched to discrete decisions.

Direct estimation alone does not solve the search problem when a fine action grid is large. We therefore place it inside a Top-KK coarse-to-fine search:

evaluate candidates⟶rank⟶retain Top-​K⟶refine.\boxed{\text{evaluate candidates}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{rank}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{retain Top-}K\;\longrightarrow\;\text{refine}.}

The method keeps cumulative cost/time statistics and operates each active action in contiguous blocks. Retaining several parents is important because a coarse action need not be attractive for its own current-grid objective value in order for its descendants to contain the eventual fine-grid optimizer. We formalize this idea through a guardian: a parent whose descendants contain a master-grid optimizer.

The resulting contribution has two interacting components: a statistical foundation for direct cost-rate estimation on a persistent trajectory, and a search mechanism that protects promising refinement regions from irreversible early deletion. The main statistical difficulty is the persistence of the queueing state. For cycle tt, let ata_{t} be the selected action, TtT_{t} its random duration, and GtG_{t} its realized cost. Our analysis starts from

Gt−f⁡(at)​Tt=conditional transient contribution+martingale innovation.G_{t}-f(a_{t})T_{t}=\text{conditional transient contribution}+\text{martingale innovation}.

The transient term need not vanish cycle by cycle. Instead, we ask whether its accumulated contribution is negligible relative to the total time spent under an action. For regenerative queues, a bias-function representation makes these transient terms telescope over contiguous action blocks, leaving only block-boundary contributions. Thus the learning cycles themselves need not be regeneration cycles and the queue need not be reset.

This transient issue is not absent from the closest gradient-based literature. GOLiQ explicitly separates regret caused by nonstationarity from regret caused by suboptimal decisions and uses increasing cycle lengths to control transient bias; LiQUAR likewise uses warm-up/overtime treatment in its performance estimation. Our distinction is therefore not that transient queueing data are unique to the present paper. Rather, we analyze a different statistical object: the direct cost-rate SAA itself. The resulting transient-bias/martingale decomposition supports objective consistency and, through ranking, hierarchical optimization rather than a gradient update.

The paper makes four main contributions, ordered from estimation to search and then to empirical scope.

  1. (i)

    We formulate a direct ratio-of-totals SAA estimator for fixed-DD operating cycles on a single persistent queue trajectory and derive an exact error decomposition into accumulated conditional transient bias and martingale fluctuation. This yields actionwise and finite-action uniform consistency.

  2. (ii)

    We give queueing-specific sufficient conditions for that consistency. For regenerative queues, bias-function boundary terms telescope within contiguous blocks of a fixed action. Martingale averaging, selected-cycle moment conditions, and a common Lyapunov route then provide fixed-DD verification without resetting the queue.

  3. (iii)

    We develop a fixed-depth Top-KK CTF method and its retention theory. A finite-sample blocked-SAA lemma handles horizon-dependent stage budgets with Lyapunov-weighted innovation variance. A guardian-separation condition then bounds irreversible pruning across stages, while a common-active-set comparison quantifies the margin advantage over Top-1. Convexity, differentiability, and gradient information are not assumed; mixed discrete–continuous controls are therefore handled without a continuous relaxation. A worked M/M/1M/M/1 workload model verifies the common drift, Poisson representation, cycle-reward moments, and completed-stage sampling conditions. For its four-level benchmark hierarchy, an exhaustive audit also verifies positive guardian margins over every required active set. The same hierarchy supplies a deterministic example in which exact-objective Top-1 discards the branch containing the master-grid optimizer while Top-KK retains it.

  4. (iv)

    We evaluate where this architecture helps and where it does not. On the LiQUAR benchmark with exact workload observations and corrected evaluation-domain projection, Top-KK has a terminal-policy identification advantage in the reported samples, while the corrected LiQUAR comparator has lower median cumulative learning cost at the large budget. In an integer-staffing M/M/sM/M/s problem, Top-KK has lower mean terminal gaps and higher optimizer-selection frequencies than Top-1 refinement and flat direct SAA at all three approximately matched operating-time budgets in a canonical 200-replication experiment. A nonpreemptive lognormal-service M/G/sM/G/s extension, with different objective geometry and retention settings, shows slower finite-horizon stabilization but sharp terminal identification once the operating horizon is sufficiently long. Finally, on the smooth GOLiQ benchmark, the specialized gradient method is substantially more efficient, identifying a regime in which available sensitivity structure should be exploited.

1.1 Related literature and positioning

Two important recent advances in online queueing optimization, and the closest papers to our setting, are GOLiQ [1] and LiQUAR [2]. Both operate queues in successive cycles and explicitly address transient data. Their optimization mechanism is gradient based: GOLiQ exploits queueing sensitivity formulas, whereas LiQUAR compares two perturbations around a continuously updated center. The present method stops one layer earlier: it estimates steady-state objective values directly and uses ranking and structured refinement. This distinction matters when controls are discrete or mixed, when the objective is nonsmooth or nonconvex, or when constructing a reliable model-specific gradient is undesirable.

Queueing bandits address partial feedback and exploration with unknown service rates, prices, or rewards; examples include [4, 3]. Our finite-grid problem also has partial feedback, but its basic observation is a steady-state cost-rate SAA contaminated by inherited-state transients rather than an i.i.d. arm reward. Top-KK pruning is used to preserve refinement paths and concentrate later operating time, not to construct a UCB index.

The work is also related to simulation optimization and steady-state estimation. Single-run steady-state optimization for queues has a long history; see, for example, [6, 8]. Regenerative simulation [5, 7] motivates our bias-function construction. Classical sample-average approximation for stochastic discrete optimization is developed in [9], while extensions to dependent data include [10, 12]. The distinguishing feature here is that dependence is generated by an adaptive control sequence and the same action may be revisited in multiple persistent operating blocks.

The positioning is therefore deliberately integrative. Direct SAA, regenerative analysis, and multiresolution search are not individually claimed to be new. The contribution is to connect them on one persistent controlled trajectory: queueing structure validates the direct estimator, the estimator drives a Top-KK hierarchy, and guardian separation translates ranking accuracy into protection against irreversible loss of an optimal refinement path. This connection also identifies the method’s natural boundary: when accurate local sensitivity information is available and the decision space is smooth, a specialized gradient method may be preferable.

The remainder is organized around the operational method. Section 2 defines persistent fixed-event-count sampling and the direct estimator. Section 3 gives the finite-budget Top-KK procedure before the technical analysis. Section 4 develops direct-SAA consistency, queueing verification, and guardian-retention theory. Section 5 reports implementation validation and four benchmark families. Section 6 discusses scope, limitations, and the distinction between terminal identification and cumulative regret.

2 Persistent Queueing Control and Direct SAA

We begin with a nonempty finite feasible action set, supplied to the learner,

𝒜={a1,…,aM},M≥1.\mathcal{A}=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{M}\},\qquad M\geq 1.

The action set may arise, for example, from a finite discretization of an underlying continuous decision space. For each a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, assume that its specified fixed-action dynamics admit a well-defined steady-state regime with finite expected cost rate f⁡(a)∈ℝf(a)\in\mathbb{R}. Identifying a feasible set from unknown queueing primitives is a separate problem; the present search operates within the supplied set. Conditions controlling the trajectory under adaptive switching are stated separately in the theoretical results. The finite-action optimization problem is therefore

a𝒜∗∈argmina∈𝒜f​(a).a_{\mathcal{A}}^{*}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal{A}}f(a). (1)

We organize the operating trajectory into successive learning cycles. Each cycle contains a fixed positive integer number DD of designated queueing events, with the counting convention fixed before learning. Depending on the application, these events may be external arrivals, admitted customers, service entries, service completions, or departures from the system. In a queueing network, they may also be completions or departures at a designated node. Thus, throughout the present development,

Dt≡D.D_{t}\equiv D. (2)

Although the number of designated events is fixed, the corresponding clock-time duration is random and may depend on the action being implemented. We use a simple, nonexplosive designated-event stream and require that the DDth subsequent counted event occurs in positive finite time almost surely under every admissible action and inherited state used in the analysis. An action that prevents the counted event from occurring is not admissible for that cycle convention, even if its stationary cost is finite. Simultaneous physical events require a specified counting and ordering rule consistent with these conditions.

The queue is observed along a single persistent trajectory. By persistent operation, we mean that the physical system is not reset between learning cycles: the terminal state of one cycle becomes the initial state of the next, even when the selected action changes. Consequently, observations collected under a given action may begin from states generated partly under previously implemented actions.

Let XtX_{t} denote a complete physical state at the end of cycle tt, with X0X_{0} the initial state. Thus Xt−1X_{t-1} is inherited by cycle tt. Depending on the model, this state may include residual service requirements, arrival ages or residual arrival information, and legacy staffing. Queue length alone need not suffice. The learner is not required to observe every state component.

Let 𝒪t\mathcal{O}_{t} be the learner’s observed history through cycle tt, including policy randomization available before the next action is selected. For analysis, use a filtration {ℋt}t≥0\{\mathcal{H}_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} containing 𝒪t\mathcal{O}_{t} and XtX_{t}. Conditional evolution, moment bounds, and martingale identities are imposed with respect to this specified analysis filtration. An enlargement of the observed history must preserve the conditional laws used in the relevant result; future primitive randomness is not included merely because a simulator can generate it in advance. At the beginning of cycle tt, an action

at∈𝒜a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}

is selected using 𝒪t−1\mathcal{O}_{t-1}. Thus ata_{t} is both 𝒪t−1\mathcal{O}_{t-1}- and ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1}-measurable. The selected action is held fixed throughout cycle tt.

Each cycle excludes its initial boundary event and includes its terminating designated event. The terminal state is recorded after that event, before the next action is selected. The model must specify how a new action affects unfinished work, admissions, residual arrival information, and any immediate service starts. All fixed-action continuation laws below use this same inherited-state and switching convention. Persistence alone does not specify these dynamics. The examples have no separate lump switching fee; introducing one would require including it exactly once in the cycle cost and verifying the corresponding bias decomposition or negligible accumulated contribution.

Let

Tt>0T_{t}>0

denote the realized clock duration of cycle tt, and let

GtG_{t}

Both TtT_{t} and GtG_{t} generally depend on the selected action ata_{t}, on the state inherited at the beginning of the cycle, and on the stochastic evolution of the system during the cycle. We suppress this dependence in the notation and write simply TtT_{t} and GtG_{t}. For every deterministic cycle index tt of the policy under analysis, assume

0<Tt<∞almost surely,𝔼⁡[Tt+|Gt|]<∞.0<T_{t}<\infty\quad\hbox{almost surely},\qquad\mathbb{E}[T_{t}+|G_{t}|]<\infty.

f^n​(a)=Cn​(a)Sn​(a)=∑t=1nIt​(a)​Gt∑t=1nIt​(a)​Tt.\widehat{f}_{n}(a)=\frac{C_{n}(a)}{S_{n}(a)}=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)G_{t}}{\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)T_{t}}. (6)

Remark 2.1 (Unknown primitives and imperfect cost observation).

The direct estimator requires realized operating times and realized costs, not an analytical formula for f⁡(a)f(a). Thus arrival-rate functions, service-time distributions, and other queueing primitives may be unknown provided their realized consequences are reflected in GtG_{t}. More generally, suppose the learner observes

G~t=Gt+Et,\widetilde{G}_{t}=G_{t}+E_{t},

instead of GtG_{t}, where EtE_{t} denotes the observation or approximation error in the realized cost for cycle tt. For the infinite-trajectory results, suppose that, for every action under consideration,

∑t=1nIt​(a)​EtSn​(a)⟶0almost surely.\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)E_{t}}{S_{n}(a)}\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{almost surely}.

Whenever the hypotheses of the corresponding almost-sure consistency result hold for the actual selection policy, its conclusion then also holds for the estimator formed from G~t\widetilde{G}_{t}. All sums and hypotheses refer to the trajectory generated by that policy, including its use of imperfect observations. The increasing-budget stagewise results require the separate condition in Remark 4.11.

From direct estimation to search.

For a small finite set, one can simply sample every action deeply and return an empirical leader. On a fine grid this becomes expensive because each action requires actual queue operation. The next section therefore uses the same estimator as a ranking primitive inside a fixed-depth refinement hierarchy. The practical algorithm requires only cumulative costs, operating times, and comparisons among active actions.

3 Top-KK Coarse-to-Fine Learning

A direct objective estimator is useful only if it can be embedded in an efficient search. The proposed CTF architecture is intentionally simple: active controls are operated in blocks, ranked by direct SAA, pruned, and refined. Earlier observations of a surviving control are retained rather than discarded.

Why Top-KK?

The Top-KK rule is intended as a middle ground between exhaustive refinement and greedy Top-1 refinement. Refining every active action avoids irreversible pruning but can require operating a rapidly growing number of fine-grid controls on the persistent queue trajectory. At the other extreme, retaining only the current empirical best action is inexpensive but can discard a coarse action whose descendants contain the eventual fine-grid optimizer. Top-KK retention reduces the candidate set while preserving several promising refinement paths. It also fits naturally with direct SAA: only objective estimates and rankings are required, without confidence bounds, gradients, or additional stochastic-approximation machinery. The guardian analysis in Section 4 formalizes when the retained set is large enough to preserve a path to a master-grid optimizer.

3.1 Finite-budget Top-K CTF procedure

The procedure samples only actions in 𝒰\mathcal{U} and targets the best action on the master grid 𝒰L\mathcal{U}_{L}. Shared children are included only once in each active set, and an action that reappears keeps its cumulative statistics. Cycle, event, and elapsed-time budgets.

Let σℓ,N\sigma_{\ell,N} be the number of completed primitive cycles at the stage-ℓ\ell ranking. Nondecreasing targets and reuse of observations imply

σℓ,N≤|𝒰|​mℓ,N.\sigma_{\ell,N}\leq|\mathcal{U}|m_{\ell,N}.

Together with almost-sure completion of each primitive cycle, this ensures completion of every prescribed finite schedule. Its designated-event count is D​σL,ND\sigma_{L,N} and its random elapsed operating time is

HN:=∑t=1σL,NTt(N).H_{N}:=\sum_{t=1}^{\sigma_{L,N}}T_{t}^{(N)}.

Here Tt(N)T_{t}^{(N)} is the duration of cycle tt in schedule NN. Thus a cycle cap bNcycb_{N}^{\rm cyc} or designated-event cap bNevtb_{N}^{\rm evt} can be respected by choosing targets with |𝒰|​mL,N≤bNcyc|\mathcal{U}|m_{L,N}\leq b_{N}^{\rm cyc} or D​|𝒰|​mL,N≤bNevtD|\mathcal{U}|m_{L,N}\leq b_{N}^{\rm evt}, respectively. These bounds are conservative. Elapsed-time comparisons use the resulting random HNH_{N}; a hard clock-time cutoff is a different stopping rule, discussed after Theorem 4.3.

This procedure is gradient free. Convexity and differentiability of ff are not algorithmic requirements. The price of this generality is that successful refinement depends on a ranking-separation condition: an action whose descendants contain a final optimizer must not be outranked by KℓK_{\ell} or more competing non-guardian actions at a pruning stage.

Choosing the retention counts without knowing ff.

The algorithm can be run with retention counts specified before observing the unknown objective: they express the breadth of refinement that the sampling budget can afford. A budgeted pilot or sensitivity comparison can inform this choice, provided its operating cost is counted. Such choices do not by themselves certify the guardian-margin condition. That condition depends on true parent costs and on which descendants are optimal. Without a relation between parent values and descendant quality, a gap between observed coarse estimates cannot certify that a pruned region contains no better descendant. We therefore distinguish a usable fixed-KK algorithm from a guarantee that a particular KK preserves an optimizer. The latter requires the structural margin hypothesis, an appropriate audit, or additional coarse-to-fine bounds. Retaining all parents avoids this pruning risk but increases sampling cost.

Operational interpretation of a guardian.

At a coarse level, a parent represents a region rather than merely its own current-grid point. We call a parent a guardian when that region contains a refinement path to a master-grid optimizer. A guardian need not itself be the best coarse action. Top-KK is useful precisely when several attractive non-guardian parents can outrank the best guardian, either because coarse discretization distorts descendant quality or because finite-sample SAA rankings are noisy.

4 Theoretical Guarantees

The analysis has three layers. First, direct-SAA error is separated into accumulated transient bias and martingale fluctuation. Second, queueing structure is used to verify that these errors are negligible under persistent fixed-DD operation. Third, stagewise SAA accuracy is converted into hierarchical optimization through guardian retention. The first two layers provide almost-sure foundations for direct SAA under persistent sampling; they are not an almost-sure convergence claim for a finite run that permanently discards actions. Section 4.3.1 instead analyzes the implemented pruning scheme through finite-sample bounds and a family of experiments whose stage targets grow across the prescribed schedules.

The principal results can be read in that order. Theorem  4.1 establishes consistency of the direct ratio-of-totals estimator. Theorem 4.2 explains how contiguous action blocks reduce regenerative transient effects to boundary terms. Lemma 4.2 supplies the finite-sample stagewise ranking bound used by Theorem 4.3. Proposition 4.3 then isolates the structural Top-KK versus Top-1 margin comparison, and Proposition  4.4 closes the assumptions for the specified M/M/1M/M/1 workload implementation. Thus the section moves from estimator validity, to queueing verification, to hierarchical decision quality.

4.1 Direct-SAA consistency on a persistent trajectory

4.1.1 Conditional transient-bias decomposition

For cycle tt, define the conditional transient term

βt:=𝔼⁡[Gt−f⁡(at)​Tt∣ℋt−1].\beta_{t}:=\mathbb{E}\left[G_{t}-f(a_{t})T_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}\right]. (7)

Since ata_{t} is ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1}-measurable,

βt=𝔼⁡[Gt∣ℋt−1]−f⁡(at)​𝔼​[Tt∣ℋt−1].\beta_{t}=\mathbb{E}[G_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}]-f(a_{t})\mathbb{E}[T_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}]. (8)

Thus βt\beta_{t} measures the predictable discrepancy between the expected cost accumulated during the actual finite cycle and the cost predicted by the steady-state rate f⁡(at)f(a_{t}) over the corresponding operating time. Because the initial state of the cycle is inherited from the preceding system evolution, this discrepancy represents the finite-cycle transient, or boundary, effect.

Define

Mt:=Gt−f⁡(at)​Tt−βt.M_{t}:=G_{t}-f(a_{t})T_{t}-\beta_{t}. (9)

By construction,

𝔼⁡[Mt∣ℋt−1]=0.\mathbb{E}[M_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}]=0. (10)

Hence

Gt=f⁡(at)​Tt+βt+Mt.G_{t}=f(a_{t})T_{t}+\beta_{t}+M_{t}. (11)

For any fixed a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, multiplying (11) by It​(a)I_{t}(a) and summing over t=1,…,nt=1,\ldots,n gives

Cn​(a)=f⁡(a)​Sn​(a)+∑t=1nIt​(a)​βt+∑t=1nIt​(a)​Mt.C_{n}(a)=f(a)S_{n}(a)+\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)\beta_{t}+\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)M_{t}.

Therefore, whenever Sn​(a)>0S_{n}(a)>0,

f^n​(a)−f⁡(a)=∑t=1nIt​(a)​βtSn​(a)+∑t=1nIt​(a)​MtSn​(a).\widehat{f}_{n}(a)-f(a)=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)\beta_{t}}{S_{n}(a)}+\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)M_{t}}{S_{n}(a)}. (12)

The two terms in (12) have distinct roles: the first represents accumulated transient bias, while the second represents zero-mean stochastic fluctuation.

4.1.2 Consistency of the direct SAA estimator

We first state a basic consistency result under abstract conditions on the two terms in (12). Sufficient conditions that are more directly verifiable in queueing models will be developed subsequently.

Theorem 4.1 (Consistency of the direct SAA estimator).

Fix an action a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}. Suppose that the following conditions hold almost surely.

(A1) The cumulative operating time diverges:

Sn​(a)⟶∞.S_{n}(a)\longrightarrow\infty. (13)

(A2) The accumulated conditional transient term is negligible relative to the cumulative operating time:

∑t=1nIt​(a)​βtSn​(a)⟶0.\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)\beta_{t}}{S_{n}(a)}\longrightarrow 0. (14)

(A3) The accumulated martingale innovation is negligible relative to the cumulative operating time:

∑t=1nIt​(a)​MtSn​(a)⟶0.\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)M_{t}}{S_{n}(a)}\longrightarrow 0. (15)

Then

f^n​(a)⟶f⁡(a)almost surely.\widehat{f}_{n}(a)\longrightarrow f(a)\qquad\text{almost surely}. (16)
Proof.

By (A1), Sn​(a)>0S_{n}(a)>0 for all sufficiently large nn, so the estimator and the normalized error decomposition are eventually well defined. Then (12) together with (A2)–(A3) gives f^n​(a)−f​(a)→0\widehat{f}_{n}(a)-f(a)\to 0 almost surely. ∎

Remark 4.1 (Discussion of the assumptions).

Condition (A1) is an information-accumulation requirement: action aa must be operated for an unbounded amount of total clock time.

Condition (A2) controls the systematic transient effect associated with persistent operation. Importantly, it does not require the individual terms βt\beta_{t} to converge to zero. Individual fixed-DD cycles may remain transiently biased; what is required is only that their accumulated contribution become negligible per unit of total operating time under action aa.

Condition (A3) concerns stochastic fluctuation rather than systematic bias. Since

𝔼⁡[Mt∣ℋt−1]=0,\mathbb{E}[M_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}]=0,

it is a martingale law-of-large-numbers condition. Under suitable moment conditions and sufficient repeated sampling of action aa, (A3) can be verified using standard martingale strong-law arguments.

An important point is that Theorem 4.1 does not require the number of designated events per cycle to increase with nn. Thus the fixed-cycle construction Dt≡DD_{t}\equiv D is admissible. Fixing DD, however, does not by itself eliminate transient bias. Because the queue is not reset between cycles, each cycle begins from an inherited state, and the corresponding transient term βt\beta_{t} need not vanish as t→∞t\to\infty. Condition (A2) requires only that, for each action aa, these transient contributions become negligible after accumulation and normalization by the total operating time Sn​(a)S_{n}(a).

Subsection 4.2 develops queueing-specific sufficient conditions for (A2) and (A3). Martingale arguments are used to control the stochastic fluctuation in (A3), while a regenerative bias representation is used to show how transient contributions in (A2) telescope over contiguous operating blocks of a fixed action.

4.1.3 Uniform consistency and empirical-leader identification

Because the action set 𝒜\mathcal{A} is finite, actionwise consistency immediately implies uniform consistency over 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

Corollary 4.1 (Uniform consistency over a finite action set).

Suppose that the conditions of Theorem 4.1 hold for every a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}. Then

maxa∈𝒜⁡|f^n​(a)−f⁡(a)|⟶0almost surely.\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\left|\widehat{f}_{n}(a)-f(a)\right|\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{almost surely}. (17)
Proof.

For every a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, Theorem 4.1 gives

f^n​(a)−f⁡(a)⟶0almost surely.\widehat{f}_{n}(a)-f(a)\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{almost surely}.

Since 𝒜\mathcal{A} is finite, these finitely many almost-sure convergence events have probability one jointly, and on their intersection the maximum of the finitely many absolute errors also converges to zero. ∎

Define the optimal value over the finite action set by

f𝒜∗:=mina∈𝒜⁡f⁡(a),f_{\mathcal{A}}^{*}:=\min_{a\in\mathcal{A}}f(a), (18)

and let

𝒜∗:={a∈𝒜:f⁡(a)=f𝒜∗}\mathcal{A}^{*}:=\left\{a\in\mathcal{A}:f(a)=f_{\mathcal{A}}^{*}\right\} (19)

denote the set of optimal actions.

Whenever Sn​(a)>0S_{n}(a)>0 for every a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, define an empirical leader by

a^n∈argmina∈𝒜f^n​(a).\widehat{a}_{n}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\widehat{f}_{n}(a).

Under the assumptions of Corollary 4.1, the empirical leader is therefore well defined for all sufficiently large nn, almost surely.

Corollary 4.2 (Consistency of the empirical leader).

Suppose that the conditions of Theorem 4.1 hold for every a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}. Then, almost surely,

a^n∈𝒜∗for all sufficiently large ​n.\widehat{a}_{n}\in\mathcal{A}^{*}\qquad\text{for all sufficiently large }n. (20)

In particular, if the finite-action problem has a unique optimizer a𝒜∗a_{\mathcal{A}}^{*}, then

a^n=a𝒜∗for all sufficiently large ​n,almost surely.\widehat{a}_{n}=a_{\mathcal{A}}^{*}\qquad\text{for all sufficiently large }n,\quad\text{almost surely}. (21)
Proof.

If every action is optimal, then 𝒜∗=𝒜\mathcal{A}^{*}=\mathcal{A}, and the conclusion is immediate. Otherwise, since 𝒜\mathcal{A} is finite, the optimality gap

Δ𝒜:=mina∉𝒜∗⁡{f⁡(a)−f𝒜∗}\Delta_{\mathcal{A}}:=\min_{a\notin\mathcal{A}^{*}}\left\{f(a)-f_{\mathcal{A}}^{*}\right\} (22)

is strictly positive.

By Corollary 4.1, almost surely there exists a finite random index NN such that, for all n≥Nn\geq N,

maxa∈𝒜⁡|f^n​(a)−f⁡(a)|<Δ𝒜2.\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\left|\widehat{f}_{n}(a)-f(a)\right|<\frac{\Delta_{\mathcal{A}}}{2}.

Fix such an nn. For any a∉𝒜∗a\notin\mathcal{A}^{*},

f^n​(a)>f⁡(a)−Δ𝒜2≥f𝒜∗+Δ𝒜2.\widehat{f}_{n}(a)>f(a)-\frac{\Delta_{\mathcal{A}}}{2}\geq f_{\mathcal{A}}^{*}+\frac{\Delta_{\mathcal{A}}}{2}.

On the other hand, for any a∗∈𝒜∗a^{*}\in\mathcal{A}^{*},

f^n​(a∗)<f𝒜∗+Δ𝒜2.\widehat{f}_{n}(a^{*})<f_{\mathcal{A}}^{*}+\frac{\Delta_{\mathcal{A}}}{2}.

Hence no action outside 𝒜∗\mathcal{A}^{*} can minimize f^n​(⋅)\widehat{f}_{n}(\cdot). Therefore

a^n∈𝒜∗\widehat{a}_{n}\in\mathcal{A}^{*}

for all sufficiently large nn, almost surely. If 𝒜∗={a𝒜∗}\mathcal{A}^{*}=\{a_{\mathcal{A}}^{*}\}, the unique-optimum conclusion follows immediately. ∎

Remark 4.2 (Finite-action versus continuous optimality).

Corollary 4.2 establishes identification of an optimizer over the finite action set 𝒜\mathcal{A}. When 𝒜\mathcal{A} discretizes an underlying continuous decision space, an additional discretization error remains. This error is treated separately in the continuous-space approximation analysis of the coarse-to-fine procedure.

4.2 Queueing verification of the direct-SAA conditions

The preceding results isolate the two quantities that must be controlled: accumulated transient bias and martingale fluctuation. We now give queueing-specific sufficient conditions. The main device is a regenerative bias representation that is compatible with fixed-DD learning cycles even though those learning cycles are not regeneration cycles. The resulting boundary terms telescope within contiguous operating blocks, while standard martingale averaging controls centered fluctuations.

4.2.1 Martingale averaging over adaptively selected cycles

We next give a convenient sufficient condition for the martingale requirement (A3). For a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, let

Nn​(a):=∑t=1nIt​(a)N_{n}(a):=\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a) (23)

denote the number of times action aa has been selected up to cycle nn.

For k≥1k\geq 1, define

τk​(a):=inf{t≥1:Nt​(a)=k},\tau_{k}(a):=\inf\{t\geq 1:N_{t}(a)=k\}, (24)

with the convention that inf∅=∞\inf\varnothing=\infty. Thus τk​(a)\tau_{k}(a) is the cycle index of the kk-th selection of action aa, whenever that selection occurs.

The following lemma is stated for a generic martingale-difference sequence, so that it can be used for more than one stochastic-error term in the subsequent analysis.

Lemma 4.1 (Martingale averaging along selected cycles).

Let {Zt}t≥1\{Z_{t}\}_{t\geq 1} be adapted to {ℋt}t≥0\{\mathcal{H}_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} and satisfy

𝔼⁡[Zt∣ℋt−1]=0,t≥1.\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}]=0,\qquad t\geq 1. (25)

Fix a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}. Suppose that, almost surely,

(M1) action aa is selected infinitely often, in the sense that

Nn​(a)⟶∞as ​n→∞.N_{n}(a)\longrightarrow\infty\qquad\text{as }n\to\infty. (26)

Under (M1), τk​(a)<∞\tau_{k}(a)<\infty for every k≥1k\geq 1 almost surely.

(M2) the average clock duration of cycles operated under aa is bounded away from zero asymptotically:

lim infm→∞1m​∑k=1mTτk​(a)>0;\liminf_{m\to\infty}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}T_{\tau_{k}(a)}>0; (27)

(M3) the conditional second moments are uniformly bounded along cycles in which action aa is selected: there exists a constant Ca<∞C_{a}<\infty such that

𝔼[Zt2∣ℋt−1]≤Caa.s. on the event {at=a},t≥1.\mathbb{E}\left[Z_{t}^{2}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}\right]\leq C_{a}\qquad\text{a.s. on the event }\{a_{t}=a\},\quad t\geq 1. (28)

Then

∑t=1nIt​(a)​ZtSn​(a)⟶0almost surely.\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)Z_{t}}{S_{n}(a)}\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{almost surely}. (29)
Proof.

Because ata_{t} is ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1}-measurable, the selection times τk​(a)\tau_{k}(a) are predictable: for every tt, {τk(a)=t}∈ℋt−1\{\tau_{k}(a)=t\}\in\mathcal{H}_{t-1}. Consequently the martingale- difference property can be evaluated at the random selected index. More explicitly, if HH is bounded and ℋτk​(a)−1\mathcal{H}_{\tau_{k}(a)-1}-measurable, then

𝔼⁡[H​Zτk​(a)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[HZ_{\tau_{k}(a)}] =∑t≥1𝔼[H𝟏{τk(a)=t}Zt]\displaystyle=\sum_{t\geq 1}\mathbb{E}\!\left[H\mathbf{1}\{\tau_{k}(a)=t\}Z_{t}\right]
=∑t≥1𝔼[H𝟏{τk(a)=t}𝔼[Zt∣ℋt−1]]=0.\displaystyle=\sum_{t\geq 1}\mathbb{E}\!\left[H\mathbf{1}\{\tau_{k}(a)=t\}\mathbb{E}[Z_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}]\right]=0.

Thus

𝔼⁡[Zτk​(a)∣ℋτk​(a)−1]=0.\mathbb{E}[Z_{\tau_{k}(a)}\mid\mathcal{H}_{\tau_{k}(a)-1}]=0.

The same predictable-index argument and (M3) give

𝔼⁡[Zτk​(a)2∣ℋτk​(a)−1]≤Ca.\mathbb{E}[Z_{\tau_{k}(a)}^{2}\mid\mathcal{H}_{\tau_{k}(a)-1}]\leq C_{a}.

Now let

𝒢k​(a):=ℋτk​(a),k≥1,\mathcal{G}_{k}(a):=\mathcal{H}_{\tau_{k}(a)},\qquad k\geq 1,

with 𝒢0​(a):=ℋ0\mathcal{G}_{0}(a):=\mathcal{H}_{0}, and define

Yk​(a):=Zτk​(a).Y_{k}(a):=Z_{\tau_{k}(a)}.

Since 𝒢k−1​(a)⊆ℋτk​(a)−1\mathcal{G}_{k-1}(a)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\tau_{k}(a)-1}, the tower property shows that {Yk​(a)}k≥1\{Y_{k}(a)\}_{k\geq 1} is a martingale-difference sequence with respect to {𝒢k​(a)}k≥0\{\mathcal{G}_{k}(a)\}_{k\geq 0} and that

𝔼⁡[Yk​(a)2∣𝒢k−1​(a)]≤Ca.\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{k}(a)^{2}\mid\mathcal{G}_{k-1}(a)\right]\leq C_{a}.

Consequently,

∑k=1∞𝔼⁡[Yk​(a)2∣𝒢k−1​(a)]k2≤Ca​∑k=1∞1k2<∞.\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y_{k}(a)^{2}\mid\mathcal{G}_{k-1}(a)]}{k^{2}}\leq C_{a}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k^{2}}<\infty.

It follows that the martingale series

∑k=1∞Yk​(a)k\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{Y_{k}(a)}{k}

converges almost surely. Kronecker’s lemma therefore gives

1m​∑k=1mYk​(a)=1m​∑k=1mZτk​(a)⟶0almost surely.\frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}Y_{k}(a)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}Z_{\tau_{k}(a)}\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{almost surely}. (30)

For m=Nn​(a)m=N_{n}(a),

∑t=1nIt​(a)​Zt=∑k=1mZτk​(a)\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)Z_{t}=\sum_{k=1}^{m}Z_{\tau_{k}(a)}

and

Sn​(a)=∑k=1mTτk​(a).S_{n}(a)=\sum_{k=1}^{m}T_{\tau_{k}(a)}.

Therefore

∑t=1nIt​(a)​ZtSn​(a)=m−1​∑k=1mZτk​(a)m−1​∑k=1mTτk​(a).\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)Z_{t}}{S_{n}(a)}=\frac{m^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{m}Z_{\tau_{k}(a)}}{m^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{m}T_{\tau_{k}(a)}}.

The numerator converges to zero by (30), while the denominator is bounded away from zero asymptotically by (M2). Since Nn​(a)→∞N_{n}(a)\to\infty by (M1), the result follows. ∎

Corollary 4.3 (A sufficient condition for (A3)).

Fix a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}. Suppose that

Nn​(a)⟶∞almost surely,N_{n}(a)\longrightarrow\infty\qquad\text{almost surely},

and

lim infn→∞Sn​(a)Nn​(a)>0almost surely.\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_{n}(a)}{N_{n}(a)}>0\qquad\text{almost surely}. (31)

Suppose further that there exists Ca<∞C_{a}<\infty such that

𝔼[Mt2∣ℋt−1]≤Caon {at=a}.\mathbb{E}\left[M_{t}^{2}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}\right]\leq C_{a}\qquad\text{on }\{a_{t}=a\}. (32)

Then

∑t=1nIt​(a)​MtSn​(a)⟶0almost surely.\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)M_{t}}{S_{n}(a)}\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{almost surely}. (33)

Thus condition (A3) of Theorem 4.1 holds.

Proof.

Apply Lemma 4.1 with Zt=MtZ_{t}=M_{t}. Condition (10) gives the required martingale-difference property, while (31) and (32) give (M2) and (M3), respectively. ∎

Remark 4.3.

The uniform conditional second-moment bound in (28) is a convenient sufficient condition rather than a minimal one. It can be replaced by more general martingale summability conditions when the cycle-level fluctuations are not uniformly square integrable. The present form is useful because it makes the distinction between information accumulation and stochastic averaging transparent.

4.2.2 Regenerative bias representation of a fixed-DD cycle

The main difficulty in verifying the transient-bias condition (A2) is that, under fixed-DD operation, individual learning cycles need not become asymptotically unbiased: each cycle begins from an inherited state. The key is therefore to represent the centered cost of each cycle as a difference of state-dependent boundary terms plus a martingale innovation. When the same action is operated over consecutive cycles, these boundary terms telescope, leaving only the states at the beginning and end of the corresponding operating block.

We now justify this cycle-level boundary representation under explicit regenerative and filtration-compatibility assumptions, without imposing a continuous-time Markov-chain or parametric distributional model. Fix an action a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, and let {ℱsa}s≥0\{\mathcal{F}_{s}^{a}\}_{s\geq 0} be the filtration used to describe its continuous operation. We require the regeneration construction to be compatible with this filtration, including the information observed by the learning procedure. Let

0<R1a<R2a<⋯0<R_{1}^{a}<R_{2}^{a}<\cdots

be almost surely finite stopping times increasing to infinity. These are the regeneration epochs strictly after time zero, even when the initial state is itself regenerative. Conditional on ℱRjaa\mathcal{F}_{R_{j}^{a}}^{a}, the next complete regenerative-cycle evolution, including its duration, cost increment, and designated-event count, is assumed to have a common law independent of ℱRjaa\mathcal{F}_{R_{j}^{a}}^{a}. The same law is assumed for the first complete cycle when the system is initialized in a regeneration state. An accessible regeneration atom with a compatible observation filtration is a sufficient setting for these requirements.

We use Xa​(s)X^{a}(s) as a complete state descriptor of the system; it need not be a CTMC. In non-Markovian queues it may include residual or elapsed interarrival and service information. Its state convention and the allocation of any costs or designated events at a regeneration epoch must agree with the filtration and cycle convention above. In particular, unconditional independence of successive cycle rewards is not a substitute for the stated conditional restart property.

Let 𝒞a​(s)\mathcal{C}_{a}(s) denote cumulative direct cost under continuous operation of action aa, normalized by 𝒞a​(0)=0\mathcal{C}_{a}(0)=0. Any initial-time charge is assigned consistently with this origin convention; costs at subsequent boundaries follow the increment convention below. Recall that the designated events are the queueing events chosen to define the fixed-DD learning cycles, such as arrivals, service completions, or departures. Let Na∘​(s)N_{a}^{\circ}(s) denote the counting process of these designated events under action aa; that is, Na∘​(s)N_{a}^{\circ}(s) is the number of designated events occurring over (0,s](0,s], with Na∘​(0)=0N_{a}^{\circ}(0)=0. The superscript ∘\circ distinguishes this event-counting process from the action-selection count Nn​(a)N_{n}(a) introduced earlier. For an ordinary regenerative cycle, define

Lja\displaystyle L_{j}^{a} :=Rj+1a−Rja,\displaystyle:=R_{j+1}^{a}-R_{j}^{a}, (34)
Yja\displaystyle Y_{j}^{a} :=𝒞a​(Rj+1a)−𝒞a​(Rja),\displaystyle:=\mathcal{C}_{a}(R_{j+1}^{a})-\mathcal{C}_{a}(R_{j}^{a}), (35)
Dja\displaystyle D_{j}^{a} :=Na∘​(Rj+1a)−Na∘​(Rja).\displaystyle:=N_{a}^{\circ}(R_{j+1}^{a})-N_{a}^{\circ}(R_{j}^{a}). (36)

By the conditional restart property,

{(Lja,Yja,Dja)}j≥1\{(L_{j}^{a},Y_{j}^{a},D_{j}^{a})\}_{j\geq 1}

are i.i.d. For this regenerative verification, assume that 𝒞a\mathcal{C}_{a} has locally finite-variation paths and define the absolute accumulated cost of a complete cycle by

Yj,absa:=∫(Rja,Rj+1a]|d​𝒞a|​(s),|Yja|≤Yj,absa,Y_{j,\mathrm{abs}}^{a}:=\int_{(R_{j}^{a},R_{j+1}^{a}]}|d\mathcal{C}_{a}|(s),\qquad|Y_{j}^{a}|\leq Y_{j,\mathrm{abs}}^{a},

where |d​𝒞a||d\mathcal{C}_{a}| is the total variation of the signed cost measure. For running costs and event charges, this accumulates the absolute running rate and the absolute cost jump at each event. Assume

0<𝔼⁡[L1a]<∞,𝔼⁡[Y1,absa]<∞.0<\mathbb{E}[L_{1}^{a}]<\infty,\qquad\mathbb{E}[Y_{1,\mathrm{abs}}^{a}]<\infty. (37)

This controls positive and negative within-cycle contributions before they cancel; integrability of the absolute net reward alone would not. The renewal-reward theorem then identifies the steady-state expected cost rate

f⁡(a)=𝔼⁡[Y1a]𝔼⁡[L1a].f(a)=\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y_{1}^{a}]}{\mathbb{E}[L_{1}^{a}]}. (38)

Consequently, the centered regenerative-cycle rewards

Zja:=Yja−f⁡(a)​LjaZ_{j}^{a}:=Y_{j}^{a}-f(a)L_{j}^{a} (39)

are i.i.d. and satisfy 𝔼⁡[Zja]=0\mathbb{E}[Z_{j}^{a}]=0. Absolute cost is used for integrability only: the rewards, residual costs, and bias function in the decomposition continue to use signed net costs.

For a state xx that can occur at a learning-cycle boundary, let σa​(x)\sigma_{a}(x) denote the time from state xx to the next strictly positive regeneration epoch. Thus, when xx is a regeneration state, this time covers one complete regenerative cycle. Let

Ba​(x):=𝒞a​(σa​(x))−f⁡(a)​σa​(x)B_{a}(x):=\mathcal{C}_{a}(\sigma_{a}(x))-f(a)\sigma_{a}(x) (40)

denote the centered cost accumulated over this residual portion of the regenerative cycle when the system is started from xx. We assume

𝔼x​[|Ba​(x)|]<∞\mathbb{E}_{x}[|B_{a}(x)|]<\infty (41)

for every possible learning-cycle boundary state. Define the regenerative bias function

ga​(x):=𝔼x​[Ba​(x)].g_{a}(x):=\mathbb{E}_{x}[B_{a}(x)]. (42)

At a regeneration state, the assumed conditional restart law gives ga=0g_{a}=0, because the ensuing full cycle has mean centered reward zero conditional on that state. This is a consequence of the compatibility assumption, not of an unconditional mean-zero cycle reward alone.

Let

τDa:=inf{s≥0:Na∘​(s)≥D}\tau_{D}^{a}:=\inf\{s\geq 0:N_{a}^{\circ}(s)\geq D\} (43)

be the random clock time required to observe DD designated events under action aa. The learning cycle itself is not assumed to begin or end at a regeneration epoch.

We also impose the following stopping-time residual-state property. For the almost surely finite stopping times τ\tau used below, whenever the centered residual cost to the next regeneration is integrable, assume

𝔼xa​[𝒞a​(R+​(τ))−𝒞a​(τ)−f⁡(a)​{R+​(τ)−τ}|ℱτa]=ga​(Xa​(τ)),\mathbb{E}_{x}^{a}\!\left[\mathcal{C}_{a}(R^{+}(\tau))-\mathcal{C}_{a}(\tau)-f(a)\{R^{+}(\tau)-\tau\}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{\tau}^{a}\right]=g_{a}(X^{a}(\tau)), (44)

where R+​(τ)R^{+}(\tau) is the first regeneration epoch at or after τ\tau. When τ\tau is itself a regeneration epoch, the residual on the left is zero and agrees with ga​(Xa​(τ))=0g_{a}(X^{a}(\tau))=0. Thus the at-or-after convention in this identity is consistent with the strictly positive regeneration time used to define BaB_{a} and gag_{a}. Away from regeneration epochs, both conventions refer to the same next regeneration. A strong Markov model with an accessible regeneration atom and compatible state, cost, and event conventions can establish this property. Strong Markovness alone, however, does not imply it for an arbitrary random regeneration state or observation filtration; (44) remains an explicit assumption here.

Proposition 4.1 (Regenerative representation of a fixed-DD cycle).

Fix a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, and suppose that, under continuous operation of action aa, the regeneration epochs and conditional restart law are compatible with {ℱsa}\{\mathcal{F}_{s}^{a}\} as specified above, and that (37), (41), and the stopping-time residual-state property (44) hold.

Assume in addition that each complete regenerative cycle contains at least one designated event,

Dja≥1almost surely,D_{j}^{a}\geq 1\qquad\text{almost surely}, (45)

and that

τDa<∞almost surely.\tau_{D}^{a}<\infty\qquad\text{almost surely}.

Suppose also that, for every possible initial state x=Xa​(0)x=X^{a}(0),

𝔼x​[|𝒞a​(τDa)−f⁡(a)​τDa|]<∞,\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[\left|\mathcal{C}_{a}(\tau_{D}^{a})-f(a)\tau_{D}^{a}\right|\right]<\infty, (46)

and that the actual centered residual cost from the terminal time to R+​(τDa)R^{+}(\tau_{D}^{a}) is integrable:

𝔼x​[|𝒞a​(R+​(τDa))−𝒞a​(τDa)−f⁡(a)​{R+​(τDa)−τDa}|]<∞.\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[\left|\mathcal{C}_{a}(R^{+}(\tau_{D}^{a}))-\mathcal{C}_{a}(\tau_{D}^{a})-f(a)\{R^{+}(\tau_{D}^{a})-\tau_{D}^{a}\}\right|\right]<\infty. (47)

Then

𝒞a​(τDa)−f⁡(a)​τDa=ga​(Xa​(0))−ga​(Xa​(τDa))+Ua​(τDa),\mathcal{C}_{a}(\tau_{D}^{a})-f(a)\tau_{D}^{a}=g_{a}(X^{a}(0))-g_{a}(X^{a}(\tau_{D}^{a}))+U_{a}(\tau_{D}^{a}), (48)

where Ua​(τDa)U_{a}(\tau_{D}^{a}) is integrable and, for every possible initial state xx,

𝔼x​[Ua​(τDa)]=0.\mathbb{E}_{x}[U_{a}(\tau_{D}^{a})]=0. (49)

The integrability conditions require finite expected absolute magnitudes for the finite-cycle and residual boundary contributions. They permit heavy-tailed models when the stated moments and the separate regeneration and residual-state assumptions hold. The learning cycles themselves need not be regenerative or independent.

Proof.

Let R+​(τDa)R^{+}(\tau_{D}^{a}) be the first regeneration epoch at or after τDa\tau_{D}^{a}. Define

KDa:=inf{k≥0:Na∘​(Rk+1a)≥D},ℛka:=ℱRk+1aa,k≥0.K_{D}^{a}:=\inf\{k\geq 0:N_{a}^{\circ}(R_{k+1}^{a})\geq D\},\qquad\mathcal{R}_{k}^{a}:=\mathcal{F}_{R_{k+1}^{a}}^{a},\quad k\geq 0.

Then R+​(τDa)=RKDa+1aR^{+}(\tau_{D}^{a})=R_{K_{D}^{a}+1}^{a} and KDaK_{D}^{a} counts the complete cycles after the initial segment ending at R1aR_{1}^{a}. The conditional restart assumption gives 𝔼x​[Zja∣ℛj−1a]=0\mathbb{E}_{x}[Z_{j}^{a}\mid\mathcal{R}_{j-1}^{a}]=0, because ℛj−1a=ℱRjaa\mathcal{R}_{j-1}^{a}=\mathcal{F}_{R_{j}^{a}}^{a}. Hence the partial sums

ℳka:=∑j=1kZja\mathcal{M}_{k}^{a}:=\sum_{j=1}^{k}Z_{j}^{a}

therefore form a martingale with respect to {ℛka}\{\mathcal{R}_{k}^{a}\}.

For every k≥0k\geq 0,

{KDa≤k}={Na∘(Rk+1a)≥D}∈ℛka,\{K_{D}^{a}\leq k\}=\{N_{a}^{\circ}(R_{k+1}^{a})\geq D\}\in\mathcal{R}_{k}^{a},

so KDaK_{D}^{a} is a stopping time for {ℛka}\{\mathcal{R}_{k}^{a}\}. Moreover,

Na∘​(RD+1a)=Na∘​(R1a)+∑j=1DDja≥D,N_{a}^{\circ}(R_{D+1}^{a})=N_{a}^{\circ}(R_{1}^{a})+\sum_{j=1}^{D}D_{j}^{a}\geq D,

and therefore KDa≤DK_{D}^{a}\leq D almost surely. Bounded optional sampling gives

𝔼x​[∑j=1KDaZja]=0.\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{K_{D}^{a}}Z_{j}^{a}\right]=0. (50)

Starting from x=Xa​(0)x=X^{a}(0), the centered cost accumulated up to R+​(τDa)R^{+}(\tau_{D}^{a}) consists of the initial residual centered cost Ba​(x)B_{a}(x) plus the stopped sum of complete centered regenerative-cycle rewards. If xx is itself a regeneration state, this initial segment is one full cycle ending at the strictly positive epoch R1aR_{1}^{a}, and its mean is ga​(x)=0g_{a}(x)=0. If τDa≤R1a\tau_{D}^{a}\leq R_{1}^{a}, then KDa=0K_{D}^{a}=0 and the sum is empty. Thus the same decomposition covers both boundary cases. Hence, by (42) and (50),

𝔼x​[𝒞a​(R+​(τDa))−f⁡(a)​R+​(τDa)]=ga​(x).\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\mathcal{C}_{a}(R^{+}(\tau_{D}^{a}))-f(a)R^{+}(\tau_{D}^{a})\right]=g_{a}(x). (51)

By the stopping-time residual-state property (44), applied at τDa\tau_{D}^{a}, the expected centered cost from τDa\tau_{D}^{a} to R+​(τDa)R^{+}(\tau_{D}^{a}) conditional on ℱτDaa\mathcal{F}_{\tau_{D}^{a}}^{a} is

𝔼xa​[𝒞a​(R+​(τDa))−𝒞a​(τDa)−f⁡(a)​{R+​(τDa)−τDa}|ℱτDaa]=ga​(Xa​(τDa)).\mathbb{E}_{x}^{a}\left[\mathcal{C}_{a}(R^{+}(\tau_{D}^{a}))-\mathcal{C}_{a}(\tau_{D}^{a})-f(a)\{R^{+}(\tau_{D}^{a})-\tau_{D}^{a}\}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{\tau_{D}^{a}}^{a}\right]=g_{a}(X^{a}(\tau_{D}^{a})). (52)

Subtracting (52) from (51) and taking expectations yields

𝔼x​[𝒞a​(τDa)−f⁡(a)​τDa]=ga​(x)−𝔼x​[ga​(Xa​(τDa))].\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\mathcal{C}_{a}(\tau_{D}^{a})-f(a)\tau_{D}^{a}\right]=g_{a}(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x}[g_{a}(X^{a}(\tau_{D}^{a}))]. (53)

Conditional Jensen’s inequality and (47) give 𝔼x​|ga​(Xa​(τDa))|<∞\mathbb{E}_{x}|g_{a}(X^{a}(\tau_{D}^{a}))|<\infty. Together with (46), this ensures that the following innovation is integrable. Defining

Ua​(τDa):=𝒞a​(τDa)−f⁡(a)​τDa−ga​(Xa​(0))+ga​(Xa​(τDa))U_{a}(\tau_{D}^{a}):=\mathcal{C}_{a}(\tau_{D}^{a})-f(a)\tau_{D}^{a}-g_{a}(X^{a}(0))+g_{a}(X^{a}(\tau_{D}^{a}))

gives (48), and (53) gives (49). ∎

Remark 4.4 (Learning cycles need not be regenerative).

The regeneration epochs are used only as an analytical device. The online learning cycles remain the fixed-DD cycles defined by the algorithm: the queue is not reset at their boundaries, and successive observations may be serially dependent through the inherited state. Thus the regenerative assumptions do not require the learning data to be i.i.d. Their role is to provide a queueing-based construction of the bias function gag_{a} and to verify the boundary representation needed for the transient-bias analysis. Condition (45) is a convenient sufficient condition ensuring that only finitely, indeed at most DD, complete regenerative cycles can be crossed during one fixed-DD learning cycle. It can be weakened whenever the corresponding stopped sum of centered regenerative-cycle rewards is integrable and has mean zero.

Remark 4.5 (GI/G/1 and other regenerative queues).

The regenerative formulation does not require exponential interarrival or service times. For example, consider a stable GI/G/1 queue under a fixed action aa. Let A1a,A2a,…A_{1}^{a},A_{2}^{a},\ldots be i.i.d. interarrival times and B1a,B2a,…B_{1}^{a},B_{2}^{a},\ldots be i.i.d. service requirements, with the two sequences independent, finite positive means, and

ρa:=𝔼⁡[B1a]𝔼⁡[A1a]<1.\rho_{a}:=\frac{\mathbb{E}[B_{1}^{a}]}{\mathbb{E}[A_{1}^{a}]}<1. (54)

An arrival that finds the system empty is a standard candidate for a regeneration construction. Its compatibility with the observed state must be specified. One convention places the restart after recording the empty-system arrival but before revealing the fresh service requirement and next-interarrival mark. Those marks then belong to the new cycle. The pre-/post-arrival state and any arrival-time costs or designated events must be assigned consistently with that convention and with the information actually available to the learner. If the state at the proposed restart already records a fresh random mark, the conditional restart law and the zero-bias normalization cannot be inferred merely from i.i.d. cycles; a compatible construction or a separate bias argument is required.

Proposition 4.1 applies only after its filtration, stopping-time residual identity, designated-event, and integrability assumptions have been checked for the chosen construction. For queue-length holding costs, the moment verification concerns the busy-cycle duration, the area under the queue-length process, and the initial and terminal residual contributions. Stronger moments of the primitive interarrival and service times can provide sufficient conditions in a particular model, but stability alone does not supply this complete verification.

The same approach is available for M/M/1, M/G/1, GI/M/1, finite-capacity, and network queues when a compatible regeneration construction and the other stated assumptions are available. These assumptions concern the analysis; the direct online SAA estimator itself requires neither observed regeneration epochs nor knowledge of the parametric forms of the arrival or service distributions.

Remark 4.6 (Connection with Poisson equations).

When the complete state process under a fixed action is Markov, the regenerative bias function in (42) is, up to an additive constant, the usual relative-value or Poisson-equation solution under standard regularity conditions. Thus the continuous-time Markov-chain Poisson formulation is a useful special case of the regenerative argument, rather than an assumption required by the learning method.

Remark 4.7 (Connection with the learning cycles).

Conditional on ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1}, both the selected action ata_{t} and the inherited initial state Xt−1X_{t-1} are known. During cycle tt, the action is held fixed at ata_{t}, and the cycle ends after DD designated events. Hence Proposition 4.1, applied conditionally with a=ata=a_{t}, yields the following identity when its regeneration and residual-state assumptions hold for every admissible action and inherited state, and the frozen-action cycle law agrees with the conditional law given the actual learning history:

Gt−f⁡(at)​Tt=gat​(Xt−1)−gat​(Xt)+Ut​(at),G_{t}-f(a_{t})T_{t}=g_{a_{t}}(X_{t-1})-g_{a_{t}}(X_{t})+U_{t}(a_{t}), (55)

where

𝔼⁡[Ut​(at)∣ℋt−1]=0.\mathbb{E}\left[U_{t}(a_{t})\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}\right]=0. (56)

Thus the cycle-level representation follows from the specified compatible regenerative construction and moment conditions, without requiring a CTMC model for the primitive queueing dynamics. A valid Poisson-equation construction of the same representation is an alternative when this particular regeneration convention is unavailable.

4.2.3 Control of transient bias through action blocks

We next develop sufficient conditions for the transient-bias requirement (A2), using the cycle-boundary state process {Xt}t≥0\{X_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} introduced in Section 2.

Fix a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}. Suppose that there exists a measurable function gag_{a} such that, whenever at=aa_{t}=a,

Gt−f⁡(a)​Tt=ga​(Xt−1)−ga​(Xt)+Ut​(a),G_{t}-f(a)T_{t}=g_{a}(X_{t-1})-g_{a}(X_{t})+U_{t}(a), (57)

where

𝔼⁡[Ut​(a)∣ℋt−1]=0.\mathbb{E}\left[U_{t}(a)\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}\right]=0. (58)

By Proposition 4.1 and Remark 4.7, this representation follows from the fixed-action regenerative construction under the conditions stated there.

Define

Δt​(a):=ga​(Xt−1)−ga​(Xt).\Delta_{t}(a):=g_{a}(X_{t-1})-g_{a}(X_{t}). (59)

Then, on the event {at=a}\{a_{t}=a\},

βt=𝔼⁡[Δt​(a)∣ℋt−1].\beta_{t}=\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta_{t}(a)\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}\right].

Define further

Rt​(a):=It​(a)​[Δt​(a)−𝔼⁡[Δt​(a)∣ℋt−1]].R_{t}(a):=I_{t}(a)\left[\Delta_{t}(a)-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Delta_{t}(a)\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}\right]\right]. (60)

Since It​(a)I_{t}(a) is ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1}-measurable,

𝔼⁡[Rt​(a)∣ℋt−1]=0.\mathbb{E}\left[R_{t}(a)\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}\right]=0. (61)

Among cycles 1,…,n1,\ldots,n, an action block for action aa is a maximal contiguous sequence of cycles during which aa is operated. Let Jn​(a)J_{n}(a) denote the number of such blocks, and write them as

[ℓa,1,ra,1],…,[ℓa,Jn​(a),ra,Jn​(a)].[\ell_{a,1},r_{a,1}],\ldots,[\ell_{a,J_{n}(a)},r_{a,J_{n}(a)}].

Then

∑t=1nIt​(a)​Δt​(a)=∑j=1Jn​(a){ga​(Xℓa,j−1)−ga​(Xra,j)}.\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)\Delta_{t}(a)=\sum_{j=1}^{J_{n}(a)}\left\{g_{a}(X_{\ell_{a,j}-1})-g_{a}(X_{r_{a,j}})\right\}. (62)
Theorem 4.2 (Vanishing transient bias under negligible action-block boundaries).

Fix a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, and suppose that (57)–(58) hold. Assume that, almost surely,

(B1) action aa is selected infinitely often and the average clock duration of its selected cycles is bounded away from zero asymptotically:

Nn​(a)⟶∞,lim infn→∞Sn​(a)Nn​(a)>0.N_{n}(a)\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_{n}(a)}{N_{n}(a)}>0. (63)

(B2) the total magnitude of the regenerative bias function at the action-block boundaries is negligible relative to the cumulative operating time:

1Sn​(a)​∑j=1Jn​(a)(|ga​(Xℓa,j−1)|+|ga​(Xra,j)|)⟶0;\frac{1}{S_{n}(a)}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{n}(a)}\left(|g_{a}(X_{\ell_{a,j}-1})|+|g_{a}(X_{r_{a,j}})|\right)\longrightarrow 0; (64)

(B3) the centered boundary fluctuations satisfy the martingale-variance summability condition

∑t=1∞It​(a)​𝔼​[Rt​(a)2∣ℋt−1]{Nt−1​(a)+1}2<∞.\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\frac{I_{t}(a)\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[R_{t}(a)^{2}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}\right]}{\{N_{t-1}(a)+1\}^{2}}<\infty. (65)

Then the accumulated conditional transient term satisfies

∑t=1nIt​(a)​βtSn​(a)⟶0almost surely.\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)\beta_{t}}{S_{n}(a)}\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{almost surely}. (66)

Hence condition (A2) of Theorem 4.1 holds.

Proof.

By (61), {Rt​(a)}\{R_{t}(a)\} is a martingale-difference sequence and Rt​(a)=0R_{t}(a)=0 whenever at≠aa_{t}\neq a. Since Nt−1​(a)+1N_{t-1}(a)+1 is ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1}-measurable, define the auxiliary weighted sequence

Vt​(a):=Rt​(a)Nt−1​(a)+1.V_{t}(a):=\frac{R_{t}(a)}{N_{t-1}(a)+1}. (67)

Then {Vt​(a)}\{V_{t}(a)\} is again a martingale-difference sequence. Condition (B3) implies

∑t=1∞𝔼⁡[Vt​(a)2∣ℋt−1]<∞almost surely,\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{E}\!\left[V_{t}(a)^{2}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}\right]<\infty\qquad\text{almost surely},

so the martingale series ∑t≥1Vt​(a)\sum_{t\geq 1}V_{t}(a) converges almost surely. At the kk-th selection of action aa, Nt−1​(a)+1=kN_{t-1}(a)+1=k. Hence the convergent series is precisely

∑k=1∞Rτk​(a)​(a)k.\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{R_{\tau_{k}(a)}(a)}{k}.

Kronecker’s lemma therefore yields

1Nn​(a)​∑t=1nRt​(a)⟶0almost surely.\frac{1}{N_{n}(a)}\sum_{t=1}^{n}R_{t}(a)\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{almost surely}. (68)

Combining this with (B1) gives

∑t=1nRt​(a)Sn​(a)⟶0almost surely.\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{n}R_{t}(a)}{S_{n}(a)}\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{almost surely}. (69)

From the definition of Rt​(a)R_{t}(a),

It​(a)​βt=It​(a)​Δt​(a)−Rt​(a).I_{t}(a)\beta_{t}=I_{t}(a)\Delta_{t}(a)-R_{t}(a).

Therefore, using the telescoping identity (62),

|∑t=1nIt​(a)​βt|Sn​(a)\displaystyle\frac{\left|\sum_{t=1}^{n}I_{t}(a)\beta_{t}\right|}{S_{n}(a)} ≤1Sn​(a)​∑j=1Jn​(a)(|ga​(Xℓa,j−1)|+|ga​(Xra,j)|)\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{S_{n}(a)}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{n}(a)}\left(|g_{a}(X_{\ell_{a,j}-1})|+|g_{a}(X_{r_{a,j}})|\right)
+|∑t=1nRt​(a)|Sn​(a).\displaystyle\quad+\frac{\left|\sum_{t=1}^{n}R_{t}(a)\right|}{S_{n}(a)}.

The first term converges to zero by (B2), while the second converges to zero by (69). This proves (66). ∎

Theorem 4.2 reduces the transient-bias problem to conditions (B2) and (B3). We next give readily verifiable sufficient conditions for these two requirements. The first route uses moment bounds only along cycles in which action aa is actually selected, together with sufficiently sparse creation of new action blocks. A subsequent result gives a queueing-oriented verification through a common Lyapunov condition.

Corollary 4.4 (Selected-cycle moments and sparse block creation).

Fix a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, and assume (B1). Recall that τk​(a)\tau_{k}(a) is the cycle index of the kk-th selection of action aa. Suppose that, for some q>2q>2,

supk≥1𝔼⁡[|ga​(Xτk​(a)−1)|q+|ga​(Xτk​(a))|q]<∞.\sup_{k\geq 1}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left|g_{a}(X_{\tau_{k}(a)-1})\right|^{q}+\left|g_{a}(X_{\tau_{k}(a)})\right|^{q}\right]<\infty. (70)

Suppose also that, for some ε∈(0,1−1/q)\varepsilon\in(0,1-1/q),

Jn​(a)​Nn​(a)1/q+εSn​(a)⟶0almost surely.\frac{J_{n}(a)\,N_{n}(a)^{1/q+\varepsilon}}{S_{n}(a)}\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{almost surely}. (71)

Then conditions (B2)–(B3) of Theorem 4.2 hold, and hence (66) follows.

Proof.

Set

Yk​(a):=|ga​(Xτk​(a)−1)|+|ga​(Xτk​(a))|.Y_{k}(a):=\left|g_{a}(X_{\tau_{k}(a)-1})\right|+\left|g_{a}(X_{\tau_{k}(a)})\right|.

Condition (70) implies supk𝔼⁡[Yk​(a)q]<∞\sup_{k}\mathbb{E}[Y_{k}(a)^{q}]<\infty. By Markov’s inequality and the Borel–Cantelli lemma,

Yk​(a)=o⁡(k1/q+ε)almost surely.Y_{k}(a)=o\!\left(k^{1/q+\varepsilon}\right)\qquad\text{almost surely}. (72)

Consequently,

max1≤i≤m⁡Yi​(a)=o⁡(m1/q+ε)almost surely.\max_{1\leq i\leq m}Y_{i}(a)=o\!\left(m^{1/q+\varepsilon}\right)\qquad\text{almost surely}.

For m=Nn​(a)m=N_{n}(a), every action-block boundary among cycles 1,…,n1,\ldots,n is either the state immediately before some selected cycle or the state immediately after some selected cycle. Therefore

∑j=1Jn​(a)(|ga​(Xℓa,j−1)|+|ga​(Xra,j)|)\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{J_{n}(a)}\left(|g_{a}(X_{\ell_{a,j}-1})|+|g_{a}(X_{r_{a,j}})|\right)
≤2Jn(a)max1≤i≤Nn​(a)Yi(a)=o(Jn(a)Nn(a)1/q+ε)almost surely.\displaystyle\qquad\leq 2J_{n}(a)\max_{1\leq i\leq N_{n}(a)}Y_{i}(a)=o\!\left(J_{n}(a)N_{n}(a)^{1/q+\varepsilon}\right)\qquad\text{almost surely}.

Together with (71), this proves (B2).

It remains to verify (B3). On the kk-th selected cycle, write

Ak​(a):=𝔼⁡[Rτk​(a)​(a)2|ℋτk​(a)−1].A_{k}(a):=\mathbb{E}\!\left[R_{\tau_{k}(a)}(a)^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{H}_{\tau_{k}(a)-1}\right]. (73)

Since Xτk​(a)−1X_{\tau_{k}(a)-1} is known at the beginning of the selected cycle,

Ak​(a)=Var⁡(ga​(Xτk​(a))∣ℋτk​(a)−1).A_{k}(a)=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(g_{a}(X_{\tau_{k}(a)})\mid\mathcal{H}_{\tau_{k}(a)-1}\right). (74)

Hence, using Var⁡(Z∣ℱ)≤𝔼⁡[Z2∣ℱ]\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid\mathcal{F})\leq\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}] and conditional Jensen’s inequality,

Ak​(a)q/2≤𝔼⁡[|ga​(Xτk​(a))|q|ℋτk​(a)−1].A_{k}(a)^{q/2}\leq\mathbb{E}\!\left[|g_{a}(X_{\tau_{k}(a)})|^{q}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{H}_{\tau_{k}(a)-1}\right].

Taking expectations and using (70) gives

supk≥1𝔼⁡[Ak​(a)q/2]<∞.\sup_{k\geq 1}\mathbb{E}[A_{k}(a)^{q/2}]<\infty.

Choose δ∈(0,1−2/q)\delta\in(0,1-2/q). Another application of Markov’s inequality and Borel–Cantelli yields

Ak​(a)=O⁡(k2/q+δ)almost surely.A_{k}(a)=O\!\left(k^{2/q+\delta}\right)\qquad\text{almost surely}.

Since 2/q+δ<12/q+\delta<1,

∑k=1∞Ak​(a)k2<∞almost surely.\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{A_{k}(a)}{k^{2}}<\infty\qquad\text{almost surely}.

At the kk-th selected cycle, Nt−1​(a)+1=kN_{t-1}(a)+1=k, and therefore this last display is exactly (B3). ∎

Remark 4.8 (Interpretation of the selected-cycle conditions).

Condition (70) is imposed only on the queue states immediately before and after cycles in which action aa is actually selected; it does not require independence of these states or of successive learning observations. The restriction q>2q>2 is useful because the same moment assumption controls both parts of the proof: the block-boundary magnitudes in (B2) and the boundary-martingale variance in (B3). Thus no separate variance-growth assumption is needed in Corollary 4.4.

Condition (71) requires new action blocks to be created slowly enough that their accumulated boundary contribution is negligible relative to operating time. By (B1), a simpler sufficient version is

Jn​(a)Nn​(a)1−1/q−ε⟶0.\frac{J_{n}(a)}{N_{n}(a)^{1-1/q-\varepsilon}}\longrightarrow 0. (75)

These are sufficient rather than necessary conditions; the direct boundary condition (B2) can hold under substantially weaker action schedules.

We next give a queueing-oriented route for verifying the preceding moment requirements along the actual adaptively controlled trajectory. The argument uses a common Lyapunov function at fixed-DD learning-cycle boundaries together with moments of the regenerative residual cost. It does not require the primitive queueing process to be a CTMC.

Let 𝖷\mathsf{X} denote the set of possible complete states at learning-cycle boundaries. For a nonnegative function 𝒱\mathcal{V} on 𝖷\mathsf{X}, define

Pa(D)​𝒱​(x):=𝔼xa​[𝒱⁡(Xa​(τDa))],P_{a}^{(D)}\mathcal{V}(x):=\mathbb{E}_{x}^{a}\!\left[\mathcal{V}\!\left(X^{a}(\tau_{D}^{a})\right)\right], (76)

where the expectation is taken when one fixed-DD cycle is run from state xx with action aa held fixed throughout the cycle.

Corollary 4.5 (Common Lyapunov and regenerative-moment verification).

Suppose that there exist a function 𝒱:𝖷→[1,∞)\mathcal{V}:\mathsf{X}\to[1,\infty), constants ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1), b<∞b<\infty, and CB<∞C_{B}<\infty, and some q>2q>2, such that, uniformly for a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A},

Pa(D)​𝒱​(x)≤ρ​𝒱​(x)+b,x∈𝖷,P_{a}^{(D)}\mathcal{V}(x)\leq\rho\mathcal{V}(x)+b,\qquad x\in\mathsf{X}, (77)

and

𝔼xa​[|Ba​(x)|q]≤CB​𝒱​(x),x∈𝖷,\mathbb{E}_{x}^{a}\!\left[|B_{a}(x)|^{q}\right]\leq C_{B}\mathcal{V}(x),\qquad x\in\mathsf{X}, (78)

where Ba​(x)B_{a}(x) is the centered residual regenerative cost in (40). Assume also that

𝔼⁡[𝒱⁡(X0)]<∞.\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{V}(X_{0})]<\infty. (79)

Fix a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} and assume (B1). Suppose that, for some ε>0\varepsilon>0,

Jn​(a)​n1/q+εSn​(a)⟶0almost surely,\frac{J_{n}(a)n^{1/q+\varepsilon}}{S_{n}(a)}\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{almost surely}, (80)

and that there exist constants ca>0c_{a}>0 and κa>2/q\kappa_{a}>2/q such that

Nn​(a)≥ca​nκafor all sufficiently large ​n,almost surely.N_{n}(a)\geq c_{a}n^{\kappa_{a}}\qquad\text{for all sufficiently large }n,\quad\text{almost surely}. (81)

Then conditions (B2)–(B3) of Theorem 4.2 hold, and therefore (66) follows.

Proof.

Remark 4.9 (Queueing interpretation of the common conditions).

Condition (77) is a uniform stability condition for the family of admissible actions at learning-cycle boundaries. Its role is stronger than merely requiring each frozen-action queue to be stable: it controls moments along the persistent trajectory generated by an adaptive sequence of actions. Conditions of this type are standard in online queueing optimization, where the admissible control set is typically kept uniformly away from the instability boundary.

The drift condition (77) is a geometric drift condition at fixed-DD cycle boundaries, not a consequence of ordinary frozen-action stability alone. In suitable light-tailed GI/G/1 settings it may be verified by a common workload Lyapunov function or by comparison with a uniformly stable dominating queue, together with the required uniform moment control. Condition (78) is a separate qqth-moment requirement on the centered residual busy-cycle cost; for queue-length holding costs this requires suitable moments of the residual busy-cycle duration and the area under the queue-length process.

For genuinely heavy-tailed primitives, such as lognormal service times, a geometric drift condition of the form (77) need not hold even though the queue is stable and many polynomial moments are finite. The corollary should therefore be viewed as one convenient verification route, especially for sufficiently light-tailed models, rather than as a general heavy-tail result. Heavy-tailed models may instead be handled through the direct conditions (B2)–(B3), the selected-cycle moment route of Corollary 4.4, or future subgeometric-drift extensions. In particular, sufficiently high finite regenerative moments alone do not imply the geometric drift condition used in this corollary.

Remark 4.10 (Why action blocks matter).

Theorem 4.2 shows that the relevant measure of persistent transient contamination is not the total number of fixed-DD cycles, but the number of separate operating blocks of action aa. Within a contiguous block, the bias-function boundary increments telescope, so only the state at the beginning and the state at the end of the block remain. Thus repeated fixed-DD cycles under the same action can accumulate arbitrarily large operating time while generating only one pair of boundary terms.

4.3 Stagewise Top-KK consistency and guardian retention

A coarse-to-fine procedure introduces a second asymptotic index: as the total schedule index NN grows, every fixed early pruning stage must itself receive more information. Otherwise a nonvanishing probability of irreversible early mis-ranking can remain. The triangular-array result below supplies a finite-sample error bound under Lyapunov-weighted variance control; the guardian theorem turns that bound into a probability of preserving a path to a master-grid optimizer. Almost-sure infinite-visit assumptions are not imposed on actions discarded in a finite-budget run.

The three terms in (102) have distinct operational meanings. The duration term prevents too little clock time from being collected despite enough completed cycles; the innovation term controls centered cycle-to-cycle noise at the data-dependent ranking time; and the boundary term charges switching between separated action blocks. The lemma is therefore the bridge between the persistent-trajectory queueing analysis and a finite-stage ranking decision. It does not yet guarantee that a useful refinement branch is retained; that step requires the guardian margin introduced below.

Nt​(a):=∑s=1tIs​(a),Lt​(a):=exp{−θ∑s=1tIs(a)Ts}ψ​(θ)Nt​(a).N_{t}(a):=\sum_{s=1}^{t}I_{s}(a),\qquad L_{t}(a):=\frac{\exp\{-\theta\sum_{s=1}^{t}I_{s}(a)T_{s}\}}{\psi(\theta)^{N_{t}(a)}}.

Conditional stochastic domination implies 𝔼⁡[e−θ​Tt∣ℋt−1]≤ψ⁡(θ)\mathbb{E}[e^{-\theta T_{t}}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}]\leq\psi(\theta). Predictability of It​(a)I_{t}(a) therefore makes Lt​(a)L_{t}(a) a nonnegative supermartingale with L0​(a)=1L_{0}(a)=1. At the bounded stopping time σ\sigma, 𝔼​Lσ​(a)≤1\mathbb{E}L_{\sigma}(a)\leq 1. On {a∈Aℓ,N,S⁡(a)<c​n​(a)}\{a\in A_{\ell,N},\ S(a)<cn(a)\}, (S2) gives

Lσ​(a)>κ​(θ,c)−n⁡(a)≥κ​(θ,c)−m.L_{\sigma}(a)>\kappa(\theta,c)^{-n(a)}\geq\kappa(\theta,c)^{-m}.

Markov’s inequality bounds this event by κ​(θ,c)m\kappa(\theta,c)^{m}; a union bound over the fixed set 𝒰\mathcal{U} proves the result. This is the standard nonnegative-supermartingale method; see [11] for its broader use. No independence after adaptive selection, and no conditioning on a random selected sample size, is required. ∎

Remark 4.13 (Poisson designated events).

If each cycle ends at its DDth external Poisson arrival, the action is held fixed during the cycle, and λ⁡(a)≤λ¯\lambda(a)\leq\bar{\lambda}, then conditional on the past TtT_{t} has law Gamma⁡(D,λ⁡(at))\operatorname{Gamma}(D,\lambda(a_{t})) (shape and rate). It dominates ξ∼Gamma⁡(D,λ¯)\xi\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(D,\bar{\lambda}). Taking c=D/(2​λ¯)c=D/(2\bar{\lambda}) and θ=λ¯\theta=\bar{\lambda} gives

ηℓ,N​(c)≤|𝒰|​exp⁡{−D⁡(log⁡2−1/2)​mℓ,N}.\eta_{\ell,N}(c)\leq|\mathcal{U}|\exp\{-D(\log 2-1/2)m_{\ell,N}\}. (111)

A simple counting process with uniformly bounded conditional event intensity admits the same argument by a Poisson envelope. For example, exponential service completions have intensity at most s¯​ν¯\bar{s}\bar{\nu} when at most s¯\bar{s} servers operate at rates at most ν¯\bar{\nu}; use Gamma⁡(D,s¯​ν¯)\operatorname{Gamma}(D,\bar{s}\bar{\nu}) as the lower bound. Batch events counted as several individual events require a different envelope. For nonexponential completion-based cycles, a suitable duration lower bound requires separate verification; ordinary service-time moments do not suffice. External-Poisson-arrival cycles avoid this residual-service issue, even with nonexponential service. Their duration verification does not, by itself, verify the other hypotheses of Lemma 4.2.

Corollary 4.6 (Stagewise consistency for increasing budgets).

Under (S1)–(S6), if

rℓ,Nmℓ,N2⟶0,jℓ,N​Λℓ,N1/qmℓ,N⟶0,\frac{r_{\ell,N}}{m_{\ell,N}^{2}}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad\frac{j_{\ell,N}\Lambda_{\ell,N}^{1/q}}{m_{\ell,N}}\longrightarrow 0, (112)

then eℓ,N→0e_{\ell,N}\to 0 in probability. The same conclusion holds under (S1)–(S5), the duration domination in Proposition 4.2, and (112).

Proof.

Each term of (102) vanishes. For the second formulation, nonemptiness of the active set gives rℓ,N≥mℓ,Nr_{\ell,N}\geq m_{\ell,N}, so the first growth condition forces mℓ,N→∞m_{\ell,N}\to\infty; then Proposition 4.2 supplies (S6). ∎

Remark 4.14 (Verification for the blocked CTF schedule).

For the algorithm in Section 3.1, the hierarchy and depth are fixed and the cumulative targets are deterministic and nondecreasing. By stage ℓ\ell, every action has at most mℓ,Nm_{\ell,N} cycles, so one may take rℓ,N=|𝒰|​mℓ,Nr_{\ell,N}=|\mathcal{U}|m_{\ell,N} and jℓ,N≤ℓ+1j_{\ell,N}\leq\ell+1. There are finitely many possible sequences of active sets and within-stage block orders, independently of NN. For each such sequence, the cycle counts at block boundaries are determined by the stage targets and the previous sampling of each action. Taking the union over all these sequences produces a deterministic covering set ℬℓ,N\mathcal{B}_{\ell,N} with Λℓ,N≤Λℓ<∞\Lambda_{\ell,N}\leq\Lambda_{\ell}<\infty, independently of NN. Its indices change with NN, but their number is bounded. Thus (112) follows from mℓ,N→∞m_{\ell,N}\to\infty even when q=1q=1. A small number of realized blocks alone would not justify this conclusion for an arbitrary adaptive within-block stopping rule.

These guarantees assume that the prescribed sampling stages are completed. A hard elapsed-time cutoff that interrupts a stage requires an additional bound on the probability of failing to reach its target; it is not covered merely by the lower-duration estimate (S6).

Remark 4.15 (Role of the almost-sure theory).

Theorem 4.1 describes an infinite operating trajectory with persistent sampling of the actions under consideration. An irreversibly pruned action in a single finite-budget CTF run does not satisfy that premise. We use the almost-sure results to explain and verify direct SAA under persistent sampling, not to assert an almost-sure guarantee for the pruning algorithm. The applicable algorithmic limit is instead Corollary 4.6: across experiments with increasing budget, every fixed stage receives increasing information before pruning. The shared Poisson/boundary decomposition connects the two analyses.

For a∈𝒰ℓa\in\mathcal{U}_{\ell}, ℓ<L\ell<L, let Chℓ⁡(a)⊆𝒰ℓ+1\operatorname{Ch}_{\ell}(a)\subseteq\mathcal{U}_{\ell+1} be the set of children generated when aa is refined. Completed schedules and clock-time cutoffs.

The bound concerns the completed prescribed schedule. A capped procedure follows the same sampling rule until completion or a hard elapsed-time cutoff tNmaxt_{N}^{\max}. The last probability requires an additional completion-time bound; the lower-duration condition (S6) does not control it. Lemma 4.2 is applied to the full run, without conditioning on completion. Clipping its ranking time at a clock cutoff does not preserve the minimum sample counts in (S2).

Corollary 4.7 (Master-grid consistency).

Suppose the hierarchy and positive guardian margins in Theorem 4.3 are fixed. If eℓ,N→0e_{\ell,N}\to 0 in probability for each ℓ=0,…,L\ell=0,\ldots,L, then

ℙ(FL,N)→1,f(a^N)−fL∗→0in probability.\mathbb{P}(F_{L,N})\to 1,\qquad f(\widehat{a}_{N})-f_{L}^{*}\to 0\quad\text{in probability}. (129)
