If any master-grid actions are suboptimal, finiteness of the grid implies that their smallest positive gap is strictly positive, so convergence of the gap to zero implies optimizer identification. If all actions are optimal, identification is immediate. ∎

Proposition 4.3 (Top-KK versus Top-1 at a common active set).

Fix ℓ<L\ell<L and an active set AA containing a guardian. For 1≤K≤K′≤|A|1\leq K\leq K^{\prime}\leq|A|,

Δℓ,K′​(A)≥Δℓ,K​(A),\Delta_{\ell,K^{\prime}}(A)\geq\Delta_{\ell,K}(A), (130)

with the convention νℓ,K=+∞\nu_{\ell,K}=+\infty if fewer than KK nonguardians exist. When both order statistics are finite, the increase equals νℓ,K′​(A)−νℓ,K​(A)\nu_{\ell,K^{\prime}}(A)-\nu_{\ell,K}(A) and is strict if these values differ. For the same vector of estimates and the same tie-breaking rule, empirical top-KK sets are nested as KK increases. Thus the event of retaining a guardian is also nested, for every realization of the estimates.

Suppose Δℓ,1​(A)<0<Δℓ,K​(A)\Delta_{\ell,1}(A)<0<\Delta_{\ell,K}(A). For estimates on this fixed set let eN​(A)=maxa∈A⁡|f^N​(a)−f⁡(a)|e_{N}(A)=\max_{a\in A}|\widehat{f}_{N}(a)-f(a)| and γ=−Δℓ,1​(A)>0\gamma=-\Delta_{\ell,1}(A)>0. If eN​(A)<γ/2e_{N}(A)<\gamma/2, Top-1 retains no guardian. If eN​(A)<Δℓ,K​(A)/2e_{N}(A)<\Delta_{\ell,K}(A)/2, Top-KK retains a guardian (automatically if its margin is infinite). Therefore, when eN​(A)→0e_{N}(A)\to 0 in probability, Top-1 loses all guardians with probability tending to one, while Top-KK keeps one with probability tending to one.

Proof.

Nonguardian order statistics are nondecreasing in KK, whereas the best guardian value is unchanged. This proves the margin ordering without subtracting infinite values. A fixed ordering of the estimated costs proves the nesting assertion. For the last claim, choose a minimum-cost nonguardian a∘a^{\circ}. Its true cost is γ\gamma below the best guardian, so eN​(A)<γ/2e_{N}(A)<\gamma/2 implies f^N​(a∘)<f^N​(g)\widehat{f}_{N}(a^{\circ})<\widehat{f}_{N}(g) for every guardian gg. Hence an empirical minimizer is a nonguardian; uniqueness of a∘a^{\circ} is unnecessary. The Top-KK claim follows from the deterministic retention argument in Theorem 4.3. ∎

Remark 4.16 (What the comparison establishes).

Top-KK can tolerate up to K−1K-1 nonguardians with costs below the best guardian. At a common active set, when both margins are positive and finite and the innovation requirement in (131) dominates, the ratio of that sufficient sample-size term for Top-KK to that for Top-1 is (Δℓ,1​(A)/Δℓ,K​(A))2(\Delta_{\ell,1}(A)/\Delta_{\ell,K}(A))^{2}, holding the other constants fixed. This is a statement about one term in a sufficient bound, not an exact sample-complexity ratio. If Δℓ,1​(A)=0\Delta_{\ell,1}(A)=0, ties can favor a guardian, so Top-1 failure cannot be concluded from a nonpositive margin alone.

Different retention schedules generate different future active-set families; their minimum margins need not be ordered. More retained parents also require more later sampling. Proposition 4.3 therefore does not imply that a complete Top-KK run outperforms Top-1 at every equal total budget. Moreover, the margins and moment constants in (131) are generally unknown: the formula explains theoretical dependence on accuracy and separation, rather than providing a calibrated data-only tuning rule.

Remark 4.17 (Scope of a guardian audit).

A positive margin along the exact-objective refinement path verifies only those active sets visited on that path. A noisy ranking can retain a different collection of parents while still keeping a guardian. Theorem  4.3 requires positive margins throughout (4.3.2), or a separately justified smaller family containing every possible guardian-preserving path. Exhaustive enumeration or a structural argument can establish this condition; one path alone cannot. For an exhaustive audit, first specify the child maps and identify the full master-grid optimal set. Compute guardians backwards through the maps, then generate (4.3.2) forwards, using every retained kℓ​(A)k_{\ell}(A)-subset that intersects the guardian set. Deduplicate active sets, but not equal costs of different actions. At each pruning level report the number of active sets checked, any automatic cases, and the minimum of the remaining margins. Terminal active sets need not be enumerated for margin verification: once the last retained set contains a guardian, the definition ensures that its children contain a master-grid optimizer.

When objective values are approximate, identifying the optimal descendants and certifying the sign of each margin require error control. In particular, a positive margin computed from simulation-based reference values alone is not a certificate for the true objective. Section 5.2 provides a full-family audit for the exact-formula M/M/1M/M/1 benchmark. The retention proof itself needs neither convexity nor differentiability, and allows overlapping descendant sets and multiple master-grid optimizers.

Remark 4.18 (Continuous-space approximation).

Suppose 𝒰L\mathcal{U}_{L} discretizes an underlying compact decision space BB and every x∈Bx\in B lies within distance δL\delta_{L} of some point of 𝒰L\mathcal{U}_{L}. If ff is uniformly continuous on BB, define its modulus of continuity by

ωf(δ):=sup{|f(x)−f(y)|:x,y∈B,∥x−y∥≤δ}.\omega_{f}(\delta):=\sup\{|f(x)-f(y)|:\ x,y\in B,\ \|x-y\|\leq\delta\}.

For x∗∈argminx∈Bf​(x)x^{*}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in B}f(x),

0≤fL∗−f⁡(x∗)≤ωf​(δL).0\leq f_{L}^{*}-f(x^{*})\leq\omega_{f}(\delta_{L}).

Hence, on FL,NF_{L,N},

f⁡(a^N)−f⁡(x∗)≤ωf​(δL)+2​eL,N.f(\widehat{a}_{N})-f(x^{*})\leq\omega_{f}(\delta_{L})+2e_{L,N}.

If ff is LfL_{f}-Lipschitz, then ωf​(δL)≤Lf​δL\omega_{f}(\delta_{L})\leq L_{f}\delta_{L}, recovering the usual Lipschitz bound. Thus even the continuous-space approximation does not require convexity. For a fixed hierarchy the result gives consistency up to deterministic grid error. If the hierarchy itself is refined with NN, both the grid radius and guardian margins may vary with NN; continuous-space consistency additionally requires stagewise estimation errors to vanish relative to the corresponding shrinking guardian margins.

4.4 A complete verification for an M/M/1 workload model

This subsection closes the theory–implementation loop for one concrete queueing model. We verify the queueing and sampling hypotheses of Lemma 4.2 for the specified persistent-workload version of the single-server model used in Section  5.2. The result is deliberately model-specific: it shows that the preceding conditions are verifiable for an implemented queue, but it is not invoked as automatic verification for the staffing or heavy-tailed experiments. The observation is integrated normalized workload. Normalized workload and queue length have the same stationary mean in this M/M/1M/M/1 model, but their sample-path integrals differ.

Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} be the finite union of the candidate grids and a=(μ,p)∈𝒰a=(\mu,p)\in\mathcal{U}. Assume

0<λ¯≤λ⁡(p)≤λ¯<μ¯≤μ≤μ¯<∞,P:=maxa∈𝒰⁡|p|<∞.0<\underline{\lambda}\leq\lambda(p)\leq\overline{\lambda}<\underline{\mu}\leq\mu\leq\overline{\mu}<\infty,\qquad P:=\max_{a\in\mathcal{U}}|p|<\infty. (132)

External arrivals have rate λ⁡(p)\lambda(p) while action aa is held fixed. Each arrival brings an independent work requirement ζ∼Exp⁡(1)\zeta\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1). Total unfinished work W⁡(s)W(s) decreases at speed μ\mu when positive and increases by ζ\zeta at an arrival. Thus under a fixed action the calendar service times are exponential with rate μ\mu. When capacity changes, the existing unfinished work is preserved and processed at the new speed; it is neither resampled nor rescaled.

Each learning cycle ends immediately after its DDth external arrival, including that arrival’s work in the terminal state XtX_{t} and charging its revenue to the action used during that cycle. The next action is chosen after this state has been observed. Future arrival randomness and work requirements are independent of the available history conditional on the selected action. The learner observes the workload and realized cost; future marks are not revealed in advance. This gives a complete state for the workload dynamics and costs, even though individual job identities are not retained. For one cycle, started from ww and run under aa, define

G=∫0TW⁡(s)​𝑑s+μ​T−p​D,f⁡(a)=λ⁡(p)μ−λ⁡(p)+μ−p​λ​(p).G=\int_{0}^{T}W(s)\,ds+\mu T-pD,\qquad f(a)=\frac{\lambda(p)}{\mu-\lambda(p)}+\mu-p\lambda(p). (133)

The first term of ff is the stationary mean workload in work units.

5 Numerical Experiments

The numerical study is designed to characterize both the advantages and the limits of direct Top-KK rather than to establish universal dominance. We first validate the event-driven implementation against queueing models with known steady-state formulas. We then ask four substantive questions. How does direct Top-KK compare with LiQUAR in terminal identification and cumulative learning cost? Does Top-KK help when controls are mixed discrete–continuous? Does the basic behavior persist in a non-Markovian heavy-tailed service model? Finally, how much can a specialized gradient learner gain in a smooth regime where reliable queueing sensitivity information is available?

Each benchmark has a distinct evidentiary role. The first separates terminal identification from cumulative learning cost in a continuous control problem; the second tests mixed discrete–continuous decisions; the third probes robustness beyond the light-tailed model verified analytically; and the fourth tests the method against a specialized gradient learner in a regime favorable to that learner. The comparisons are therefore interpreted benchmark by benchmark, with their information inputs, resource matching, and primary performance criteria stated explicitly rather than pooled into a single algorithm ranking.

All four experiments use the same logistic demand function

λ⁡(p)=10​e4.1−p1+e4.1−p.\lambda(p)=10\frac{e^{4.1-p}}{1+e^{4.1-p}}.

Under a fixed price pp, external arrivals are Poisson with rate λ⁡(p)\lambda(p). The feasible action domains, service mechanisms, staffing costs, and learning-cycle conventions are specified for each benchmark below.

Interpretation of the retention schedules and audits.

The comparisons below evaluate the specified fixed retention schedules. They do not evaluate a method that learns a sufficient KK without access to reference-objective information. Exact or high-precision reference values are used to assess refinement geometry and terminal performance. For the four-level M/M/1M/M/1 benchmark in Section 5.2, the reported margins have been independently reproduced by an exhaustive audit of (4.3.2) using the implementation’s child maps. The five-level comparison and the explicitly documented shared staffing hierarchy also admit full-family audits with exact-formula objective bounds. Their model-level sampling and moment conditions require separate verification. The lognormal family is exhaustively checked against saved reference estimates. A simultaneous Monte Carlo-error sensitivity analysis is reported below, but missing transient-bias and historical run metadata still prevent treating that check as a certificate for the true objective. These audits assess fixed retention schedules and are not inputs to the online SAA rankings.

Computational record.

The accompanying computational-provenance packages index every table and figure below. It separates full records (source, inputs, randomization, raw output, and aggregation are available), partial records (saved output is traceable but some historical metadata are missing), and archival records (only a historical summary or figure was recovered). Missing metadata are not reconstructed silently. In particular, the historical light-tailed staffing summary has been replaced by a newly specified canonical experiment with frozen configuration, independently seeded randomization and simulation streams, replication-level raw output, automated validation, and exact replay checks. This is a replacement experiment, not a reproduction of the unrecovered historical run. The final GOLiQ comparison is likewise replaced by a corrected run with independently seeded simulation streams. Section 5.6 summarizes the record and the benchmark-specific paragraphs give the detailed design information.

5.1 Implementation validation

We validated the simulators independently of the learning algorithms. For the single-server benchmark, long fixed-action runs were compared with the exact arrival rate, mean workload, and cost rate. Each fixed-DD cycle was checked to contain exactly DD designated arrivals, workload remained nonnegative, and the workload integral was evaluated analytically between event epochs. For fixed-price arrival cycles, the mean and variance of the duration are D/λ⁡(p)D/\lambda(p) and D/λ​(p)2D/\lambda(p)^{2}. At price p=3.78551p=3.78551 with D=50D=50, the theoretical mean cycle duration is 8.650818.65081 and the simulated value is 8.662388.66238; the corresponding variances are 1.496731.49673 and 1.520481.52048. Table 1 reports representative cost-rate checks. We also switched the parallel-server simulator back to exponential service and verified it against exact Erlang-C calculations before using lognormal service. For each fixed-DD M/M/1M/M/1 row, we used 20 independent replications of 2,000 cycles, with D=50D=50, an empty start, and no discarded warm-up; the reported Monte Carlo standard error is computed across replication-level cost-rate estimates. The four displayed actions use seed ranges 1000010000–1001910019, 1100011000–1101911019, 1400014000–1401914019, and 1500015000–1501915019, respectively. The separate duration check uses seed 76543217654321 on one persistent 5,000-cycle path. The M/M/5M/M/5 row is an archived validation result: its original horizon, replication count, and seed rule were not recovered.

The optimization layer was checked separately by replacing all stochastic SAA values with exact or high-precision reference objective values. This reproduces the reported master-grid optima and guardian-retention paths, so the queue simulator and the hierarchical search can be audited independently.

For the three benchmarks with analytic steady-state objectives, Table 2 summarizes the full-domain optimum f∗f^{*} and the minimum fL∗f_{L}^{*} on the stated master grid. The optima were recomputed from the objective formulas, using Erlang C for the staffing model, and by enumeration of each master grid. The full-domain staffing optimum retains integer s∈{4,…,8}s\in\{4,\ldots,8\} and optimizes only price continuously. Displayed values are rounded numerical evaluations of the analytic objectives.

For a Top-KK recommendation on the master grid, the reported terminal gap separates as

f⁡(a^)−f∗=[f⁡(a^)−fL∗]+[fL∗−f∗].f(\widehat{a})-f^{*}=\bigl[f(\widehat{a})-f_{L}^{*}\bigr]+\bigl[f_{L}^{*}-f^{*}\bigr].

The first term is the learning error relative to the grid; the second is the deterministic discretization gap, which persists even after correct master-grid identification. This decomposition does not impose the same grid restriction on a continuously valued comparator.

Costs and information available to the learners.

Table 3 distinguishes the statistics used to update each learner from the simulator’s full state and evaluation records. In the workload benchmark, W⁡(u)W(u) denotes unfinished work in mean-one work units, rather than time to clear the system. In the customer-count benchmarks, Q⁡(u)Q(u) includes customers in service. At a fixed stable action in the exponential single-server model,

𝔼⁡[W∞]=𝔼⁡[Q∞]=λ⁡(p)μ−λ⁡(p).\mathbb{E}[W_{\infty}]=\mathbb{E}[Q_{\infty}]=\frac{\lambda(p)}{\mu-\lambda(p)}.

This equality of stationary means does not identify their realized integrals or make their observation requirements interchangeable.

Direct SAA uses the resulting cycle costs and durations; it does not require latent service requirements or the analytic demand function as ranking inputs. Nevertheless, supplying the exact workload integral is an observation assumption: the workload experiment does not obtain it from completion records alone. By contrast, the staffing reward can be accumulated from customer counts, busy-server counts, arrivals, and time without knowing unfinished service requirements. The staffing row describes the documented shared model implemented by the canonical light-tailed driver and the recovered lognormal implementation. Evaluation formulas for ff and f∗f^{*} are not learning inputs for the direct-SAA methods.

Learning-cost metrics and budget accounting.

Let HH denote the completed observation horizon of one replication, C⁡(H)C(H) its realized cumulative cost, a⁡(u)a(u) the action label in force at time uu, and f∗f^{*} the continuous-domain optimum for the benchmark. We distinguish

Rreal​(H)=C⁡(H)−f∗​H,Rps​(H)=∫0H{f⁡(a⁡(u))−f∗}​𝑑u.R^{\mathrm{real}}(H)=C(H)-f^{*}H,\qquad R^{\mathrm{ps}}(H)=\int_{0}^{H}\{f(a(u))-f^{*}\}\,du. (140)

The first is realized regret: it includes inherited-state transients and sample noise and can be negative on an individual path. The second is stationary-policy pseudo-regret: it replaces realized cost on each operating interval by the stationary objective of its action label and excludes those transient and sampling effects. The corresponding rates divide by HH. Neither quantity is the terminal gap f⁡(a^)−f∗f(\widehat{a})-f^{*}, which evaluates only the final recommendation. These evaluation quantities use ff and f∗f^{*} offline; they are not learner inputs.

Every completed Top-KK primitive cycle is charged in C⁡(H)C(H) and HH, and the reported runs finish their deterministic stage targets rather than stopping at a hard clock cutoff. LiQUAR completes both full clock periods in every iteration. Its beginning and ending portions omitted from the workload update remain fully charged in realized cost and time. Thus Table 5 matches mean clock time only approximately: LiQUAR time is deterministic for a given iteration schedule, while Top-KK time is random. For the GOLiQ comparison, service entries are matched exactly within pairs; if the matched event occurs inside a GOLiQ learning cycle, cost and time through that event are charged but the incomplete cycle produces no gradient update. The three LiQUAR sensitivity settings are reported separately; no best setting is selected and no outer-loop selection cost is represented.

5.2 LiQUAR benchmark: terminal identification versus learning cost

This benchmark asks whether a direct ranking hierarchy can improve terminal policy identification without obscuring the cumulative operating cost paid during learning. We first consider the M/M/1M/M/1 logistic benchmark of Chen, Hong, and Liu [2]. Here the staffing cost is linear, and

f⁡(μ,p)=λ⁡(p)μ−λ⁡(p)+μ−p​λ​(p),(μ,p)∈ℬ:=[6.5,10]×[3.5,7].f(\mu,p)=\frac{\lambda(p)}{\mu-\lambda(p)}+\mu-p\lambda(p),\qquad(\mu,p)\in\mathcal{B}:=[6.5,10]\times[3.5,7].

On this rectangle,

0.52153<λ⁡(p)<6.45657<6.5≤μ,0.52153<\lambda(p)<6.45657<6.5\leq\mu,

so every candidate action satisfies the rate bounds of Proposition 4.4. Under that proposition’s normalized-work, switching, observation, and initialization conventions, its model-level estimation guarantee applies to the blocked Top-KK procedure. Guardian separation is verified below for its stated hierarchy. This specialization concerns the stated workload model, not a verification of the LiQUAR perturbation scheme.

For clarity, with D=50D=50 external arrivals per cycle, the Top-KK reward is

Gt=∫cycle ​tW⁡(u)​𝑑u+μt​Tt−pt​D,G_{t}=\int_{\text{cycle }t}W(u)\,du+\mu_{t}T_{t}-p_{t}D,

where WW is normalized unfinished work with mean-one work requirements. A cycle ends after the DDth external arrival, including its work and revenue. Inherited work is preserved and drains at the newly selected rate μt\mu_{t}; subsequent arrivals use the newly selected price ptp_{t}. The simulated workload integral is observed exactly here.

The exact continuous optimum is

(μ∗,p∗)≈(8.18393,3.78551),f∗≈−11.29147.(\mu^{*},p^{*})\approx(8.18393,3.78551),\qquad f^{*}\approx-11.29147.

For Top-KK, the hierarchy

3×3→5×5→9×9→17×173\times 3\to 5\times 5\to 9\times 9\to 17\times 17

has master-grid optimum (8.46875,3.71875)(8.46875,3.71875) and deterministic grid gap 0.015650.01565. We use K=(1,2,4)K=(1,2,4). The archived specifications give cumulative per-action stage targets (30,80,110,135)(30,80,110,135), (94,251,345,423)(94,251,345,423), and (236,630,867,1064)(236,630,867,1064) for the low, medium, and large budgets. The saved Top-KK raw rows and summaries are available, but their original experiment wrapper and row-level seed formula were not recovered; those rows therefore have partial rather than full computational provenance. The corrected LiQUAR side has complete source, seed lists, raw output, and probe traces in the N3 package.

Child maps and full-family guardian audit.

The archived four-level policy specifies equally spaced coordinate grids with nℓ=2ℓ+1+1n_{\ell}=2^{\ell+1}+1 points and parent mesh hℓ=3.5/(nℓ−1)h_{\ell}=3.5/(n_{\ell}-1). Its child rule is

Chℓ(μ,p)={(μ′,p′)∈𝒰ℓ+1:|μ′−μ|≤hℓ/2,|p′−p|≤hℓ/2}.\operatorname{Ch}_{\ell}(\mu,p)=\left\{(\mu^{\prime},p^{\prime})\in\mathcal{U}_{\ell+1}:|\mu^{\prime}-\mu|\leq h_{\ell}/2,\quad|p^{\prime}-p|\leq h_{\ell}/2\right\}. (141)

The implementation adds a 10−1210^{-12} comparison tolerance. All grid coordinates and half-mesh boundaries here are binary rationals, and an excluded coordinate exceeds its boundary by at least 0.218750.21875, so this tolerance leaves the displayed child sets unchanged. Midpoint children may have more than one parent; unions remove duplicate actions. Rankings break ties lexicographically in (μ,p)(\mu,p). Each level covers the next one, and all 289 master-grid actions are reachable from the initial grid.

Using these maps, we identify the unique master-grid optimizer, compute guardians backwards, and enumerate every guardian-preserving active set at the pruning levels. Table 4 gives the results. There are four guardians in each full candidate grid at these levels; the active sets need not contain all four. Every enumerated case is nonautomatic. Objective values and margin signs were checked with rational interval bounds on the exponential in the logistic formula, including a strict interval separation of the master-grid optimum. The displayed lower bounds are conservative truncations of the certified bounds.

The recomputed minima, approximately 5.237434335.23743433, 2.860342182.86034218, and 0.059677320.05967732, reproduce the saved audit values. They are full-family minima, not margins from a single exact-objective path. In particular, the exact Top-KK path has larger margins at levels 1 and 2, approximately 2.926937232.92693723 and 0.310961580.31096158. Together with Proposition 4.4, this verifies the hypotheses of Theorem 4.3 for the specified workload implementation and completed stage targets. If every mℓ,N→∞m_{\ell,N}\to\infty, Corollary 4.7 therefore gives master-grid optimizer identification in probability. The moment constants provide sufficient bounds, not calibrated predictions of the finite budgets in the tables.

Structural evidence: exact Top-1 failure.

The same hierarchy gives a concrete deterministic Top-1 failure. Exact-objective Top-1 retains (10,3.5)(10,3.5) at level 0 and (9.125,3.5)(9.125,3.5) at level 1. At level 2 its best action is again (9.125,3.5)(9.125,3.5), now a nonguardian; the best guardian is (8.6875,3.5)(8.6875,3.5), with Δ2,1≃−0.03699891\Delta_{2,1}\simeq-0.03699891. Thus Top-1 loses the master-grid optimum even with exact rankings. This geometric comparison does not imply that Top-KK has smaller error at every equal finite operating-time budget.

LiQUAR operates two perturbed controls around its current center and forms a finite-difference gradient. We use the published base schedules

ηk=4k−1,δk=min{0.1,0.5k−1/3},Tk=200k1/3,α=0.1,\eta_{k}=4k^{-1},\qquad\delta_{k}=\min\{0.1,0.5k^{-1/3}\},\qquad T_{k}=200k^{1/3},\qquad\alpha=0.1,

with nominal initial center (10,5)(10,5), projected as specified below. Our primary comparator, labeled LiQUAR-oracleW, receives exact workload observations, as does Top-KK in this benchmark. It still trims its holding-cost observations to [α​Tk,(1−α)​Tk][\alpha T_{k},(1-\alpha)T_{k}]. In the recovered implementation, its cost-rate estimate for one period under (μ,p)(\mu,p) is

f^G=−p​JTk+1(1−2​α)​Tk​∫α​Tk(1−α)​TkW⁡(u)​𝑑u+μ,\widehat{f}^{\,G}=-\frac{pJ}{T_{k}}+\frac{1}{(1-2\alpha)T_{k}}\int_{\alpha T_{k}}^{(1-\alpha)T_{k}}W(u)\,du+\mu,

where JJ counts all arrivals during that period. Thus revenue uses observed arrivals, not the analytic demand rate. Full-period costs are recorded separately for performance evaluation. Exact workload removes recoverability censoring but does not equate the methods’ time windows, cycle lengths, or update rules.

The additional delayed mode replaces W⁡(u)W(u) in this estimate by W(u)𝟏{W(u)≤μ(Tk−u)}W(u)\mathbf{1}\{W(u)\leq\mu(T_{k}-u)\}, as in [2, Section 4.2]. The published FCFS observation model reveals arrivals immediately and individual work on completion. Our simulator evaluates the equivalent recoverability statistic from its internal state; it does not implement a separate reconstruction routine using customer records. Both modes retain the same warm-up and overtime exclusions. The corrected comparisons below use these observation modes, with raw outputs, seed lists, and evaluation-control traces retained in the accompanying reproducibility package.

Evaluation controls, feasibility, and the corrected projection.

The recovered implementation uses a uniform coordinate choice ik∈{1,2}i_{k}\in\{1,2\}, Zk=2​eikZ_{k}=2e_{i_{k}}, and

xk−=x¯k−δk​eik,xk+=x¯k+δk​eik,Hk=2​eikδk​{f^G​(xk+)−f^G​(xk−)}.x_{k}^{-}=\bar{x}_{k}-\delta_{k}e_{i_{k}},\qquad x_{k}^{+}=\bar{x}_{k}+\delta_{k}e_{i_{k}},\qquad H_{k}=\frac{2e_{i_{k}}}{\delta_{k}}\{\widehat{f}^{\,G}(x_{k}^{+})-\widehat{f}^{\,G}(x_{k}^{-})\}.

It projects only the next center onto ℬ\mathcal{B}. This follows the displayed update in [2, Algorithm 1], but does not ensure that the two executed controls belong to ℬ\mathcal{B}. For example, a capacity perturbation at the initial center (10,5)(10,5) uses (10.1,5)(10.1,5), outside the stated capacity range. At center (6.5,3.5)(6.5,3.5), the possible lower probes have stability slacks

6.4−λ⁡(3.5)≃−0.0565631,6.5−λ⁡(3.4)≃−0.1818777.6.4-\lambda(3.5)\simeq-0.0565631,\qquad 6.5-\lambda(3.4)\simeq-0.1818777.

Thus stability of the center rectangle does not guarantee stability of every fixed-action evaluation. A finite operating period can still be simulated at such a control, but its stationary workload mean is not finite; the resulting adaptive path is not thereby proved to be unstable. The original numerical results must be distinguished from results under a projection that enforces the stated domain.

For the corrected implementation, let r=0.1r=0.1 and set

ℬr=[6.5+r,10−r]×[3.5+r,7−r],x¯1=Πℬr(10,5)=(9.9,5),x¯k+1=Πℬr(x¯k−ηkHk).\begin{gathered}\mathcal{B}_{r}=[6.5+r,10-r]\times[3.5+r,7-r],\\ \bar{x}_{1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_{r}}(10,5)=(9.9,5),\quad\bar{x}_{k+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_{r}}(\bar{x}_{k}-\eta_{k}H_{k}).\end{gathered}

All other update and observation conventions are retained. The archived tuning schedules are, more precisely,

ηk(c)=4c/k,δk(c)=min{0.1, 0.5ck−1/3},c∈{0.6,1,1.2};\eta_{k}(c)=4c/k,\qquad\delta_{k}(c)=\min\{0.1,\,0.5ck^{-1/3}\},\qquad c\in\{0.6,1,1.2\};

the cap is not multiplied by cc. Hence δk​(c)≤r\delta_{k}(c)\leq r in every case. Coordinatewise inclusion gives xk±∈ℬx_{k}^{\pm}\in\mathcal{B} and

μk±−λ⁡(pk±)≥6.5−λ⁡(3.5)≃0.04343694>0.\mu_{k}^{\pm}-\lambda(p_{k}^{\pm})\geq 6.5-\lambda(3.5)\simeq 0.04343694>0.

This construction preserves both the symmetry and the spacing of the finite differences. It needs only the supplied domain and perturbation cap; the demand function is used to verify the bound, not to select controls. The benchmark optimizer (8.18393,3.78551)(8.18393,3.78551) lies in ℬr\mathcal{B}_{r}, so the optimal value f∗f^{*} is unchanged. A fixed inset need not preserve the optimum of a different problem, especially one with a boundary minimizer. This is a feasibility correction, not a proof of LiQUAR convergence or an application of the fixed-arrival-count Top-KK theorem.

We retain the displayed normalization of HkH_{k} to isolate the projection change. With exact objective values, its expectation over the coordinate choice is 2∇f(x¯k)+O(δk2)2\nabla f(\bar{x}_{k})+O(\delta_{k}^{2}); thus the unprojected update has twice the leading gradient term of a convention normalized to ∇f\nabla f. No silent rescaling of the historical update is made.

The domain audit exactly reproduced all 190 saved baseline outputs from an earlier independent LiQUAR recheck. Those trajectories contained 7,874 out-of-domain evaluations, including 1,191 frozen-action-unstable evaluations. We therefore reran the comparison with the corrected projection. Across 470 corrected replications (190 oracle-workload, 190 delayed-workload, and 90 tuning runs), all 183,600 evaluations lie in ℬ\mathcal{B}; their smallest recorded stability slack is 0.143440.14344. These checks supplement the pathwise domain proof above.

Because Top-KK uses fixed-arrival-count cycles and LiQUAR uses fixed-clock periods, we compare similar mean cumulative operating times rather than iteration counts. Table 5 combines the unchanged Top-KK samples with new LiQUAR-oracleW runs using the corrected projection. LiQUAR uses 42, 100, and 200 iterations, respectively. Its mean times differ from Top-KK’s by at most about 2%2\%; this is not a comparison at identical pathwise stopping times. The reported Top-KK terminal gaps are smaller at all three budgets. The original main-table LiQUAR values and the independently reproduced rechecks are preserved separately in the revision record.

With LiQUAR’s delayed-workload statistic and the same corrected projection, the median terminal gaps are approximately 0.8610.861, 0.3790.379, and 0.1530.153 (100, 60, and 30 replications), above the corresponding Top-KK values. Top-KK retains exact workload observations in this comparison. These results are a sensitivity check for LiQUAR, not a comparison in which both learners face delayed observations. For a delayed-observation Top-KK procedure, the ranking rule must use only costs available at its decision times, and the accumulated error condition in Remark 4.11 must be verified under that actual policy. Neither this implementation nor that verification is supplied here.

At the large budget, we also reran the three previously specified settings c∈{0.6,1,1.2}c\in\{0.6,1,1.2\} with shorter periods Tk=40​k1/3T_{k}=40k^{1/3}, using 30 replications per setting and the same corrected projection. Each run has 660 iterations and total operating time about 345,107345{,}107. For c=0.6,1,1.2c=0.6,1,1.2, respectively, the median terminal gaps are 0.3540.354, 0.2070.207, and 0.2360.236. Table 6 supplies the corresponding realized learning costs, replication counts, clock-time variability, and pointwise distribution-free confidence intervals for the population median. The intervals use symmetric order statistics and have coverage at least 95%95\% under independent continuous replications; no multiple-comparison adjustment is made.

The low-budget samples favor Top-KK on median realized regret, whereas the medium- and large-budget samples favor corrected LiQUAR on that criterion. At the large budget, every reported LiQUAR setting has a larger median terminal gap but a smaller median realized regret than Top-KK. The shorter-period settings also reduce median realized regret relative to the corrected LiQUAR baseline while increasing its median terminal gap. These are unpaired comparisons at similar, not identical, time horizons. They support a finite-sample tradeoff between terminal identification and learning cost; they do not establish universal dominance or identify an optimally tuned LiQUAR policy. The three settings are reported separately, without treating their best observed value as an independently validated tuning result.

5.3 Mixed discrete–continuous staffing: an M/M/sM/M/s benchmark

This benchmark isolates the setting in which direct ranking is especially natural: one decision coordinate is integer-valued and has no ordinary gradient. Unlike the preceding continuous-capacity comparison, ordinary derivatives with respect to staffing are unavailable. We consider

s∈{4,5,6,7,8},p∈[3.5,7],ν=1.75,s\in\{4,5,6,7,8\},\qquad p\in[3.5,7],\qquad\nu=1.75,

where ss is the number of identical servers, each server works at rate ν\nu, and the arrival rate remains logistic. The steady-state objective is

f⁡(s,p)=𝔼⁡[Q∞​(s,p)]+s−p​λ​(p).f(s,p)=\mathbb{E}[Q_{\infty}(s,p)]+s-p\lambda(p).

Here Q∞Q_{\infty} counts all customers in the system, including those in service. The shared nonpreemptive staffing model uses cycles of D=50D=50 external arrivals and cycle cost

Gt=∫cycle ​t[Q⁡(u)+max⁡{st,B⁡(u)}]​𝑑u−pt​D,G_{t}=\int_{\text{cycle }t}\bigl[Q(u)+\max\{s_{t},B(u)\}\bigr]\,du-p_{t}D, (142)

where Q⁡(u)Q(u) is the total number of customers and B⁡(u)B(u) the number of busy servers. A staffing increase immediately starts waiting jobs when possible; a decrease lets existing services finish and charges legacy busy servers until completion. These immediate service starts are not counted as external arrivals. The physical state retains the active residual service requirements and the FCFS waiting work; these latent requirements need not be observed by the learner, which uses accumulated cost and time. Future arrivals use the newly selected price. These conventions define the canonical staffing model implemented by the common Top-KK/Top-1/flat driver below. For exponential service, 𝔼⁡[Q∞]\mathbb{E}[Q_{\infty}] is computed exactly from Erlang C for evaluation only. The continuous-price optimum is approximately

(s∗,p∗)=(5,3.73466),f∗=−12.97142.(s^{*},p^{*})=(5,3.73466),\qquad f^{*}=-12.97142.

The hierarchy keeps the five integer staffing values unchanged while refining only the price grid:

5×3→5×5→5×9→5×17.5\times 3\to 5\times 5\to 5\times 9\to 5\times 17.

For the hierarchy audit and the canonical driver, a parent retains its staffing coordinate and generates the next-grid prices within half the parent price mesh. Thus, with hℓ=3.5/(2ℓ+1)h_{\ell}=3.5/(2^{\ell+1}) and next-level price grid Pℓ+1P_{\ell+1},

Chℓ(s,p)={(s,p′):p′∈Pℓ+1,|p′−p|≤hℓ/2}.\operatorname{Ch}_{\ell}(s,p)=\{(s,p^{\prime}):p^{\prime}\in P_{\ell+1},\ |p^{\prime}-p|\leq h_{\ell}/2\}. (143)

Unions deduplicate shared children, and cost ties are broken by (s,p)(s,p). This rule covers every next-level grid. The master-grid optimum is (5,3.71875)(5,3.71875), with discretization gap about 0.001290.00129. For K=(2,2,2)K=(2,2,2), exhaustive enumeration gives active-set family sizes 1,27,471,27,47. All cases are nonautomatic. Rational interval evaluation of Erlang C certifies the unique optimizer and uniform margin lower bounds 0.866307560.86630756, 0.909982200.90998220, and 0.699687270.69968727, reproducing the reported margins 0.86630.8663, 0.91000.9100, and 0.69970.6997. This verifies the explicitly stated hierarchy. The stochastic implementation is checked separately through fixed-action Erlang-C comparisons, transition invariants, raw-schema and accounting validators, seed-isolation checks, and exact aggregate replay from the retained replication rows. In this example exact-objective Top-1 also reaches the master-grid optimizer, so the main role of Top-KK is statistical protection against an early noisy ranking rather than correction of a deterministic coarse-grid failure.

Table 7 reports a new canonical comparison of Top-KK, Top-1 CTF, and flat direct SAA using 200 independent replications per method and budget. All methods use the same simulator and terminal master grid. The frozen per-action stage allocations for Top-KK are (15,50,150,500)(15,50,150,500), (45,150,450,1500)(45,150,450,1500), and (120,400,1200,4000)(120,400,1200,4000) at the low, medium, and large budgets; the corresponding Top-1 allocations are (22,72,215,717)(22,72,215,717), (65,217,650,2167)(65,217,650,2167), and (166,554,1663,5543)(166,554,1663,5543). The mean operating times differ from Top-KK by −3.83%-3.83\%, −0.66%-0.66\%, and −0.65%-0.65\% for Top-1 and by +2.16%+2.16\%, +2.38%+2.38\%, and +1.96%+1.96\% for flat SAA from low to large budget. 5.4 Heavy-tailed non-Markovian service: a nonpreemptive M/G/sM/G/s test

This experiment is a robustness test, not an additional model-verification theorem. We next keep the same pricing and integer-staffing problem but replace exponential service by lognormal service with

𝔼⁡[S]=1/1.75,SCV⁡(S)=4.\mathbb{E}[S]=1/1.75,\qquad\operatorname{SCV}(S)=4.

The queue-length process alone is no longer Markovian; the complete persistent state includes residual service requirements. Staffing changes are nonpreemptive. When the target ss decreases, customers already in service finish before the corresponding servers leave, and staffing cost is charged for those legacy busy servers until completion. Its fixed-arrival cycles and signed costs follow (142); the change is the service distribution.

Because lognormal service has no finite positive exponential moment, we do not invoke Corollary 4.5 as an analytical verification for this experiment: its common fixed-DD drift assumption is geometric and need not hold in this heavy-tailed setting. The experiment is therefore presented as a numerical robustness test beyond that convenient verification route. The more general block-boundary conditions (B2)–(B3) and the selected-cycle moment route identify possible analytical avenues, but we do not claim here that those conditions have been verified for this particular M/G/sM/G/s model.

There is no Erlang-C truth for this model. The archived reference table records a mean, Monte Carlo standard error, and replication count for every point of the 5×175\times 17 master grid, with additional replications for the leading candidates. The fixed-action raw replications, seed rule, run length, and burn-in were not recovered. The reference master-grid optimum is

(sL∗,pL∗)=(5,3.9375),fL∗≈−12.44433,(s_{L}^{*},p_{L}^{*})=(5,3.9375),\qquad f_{L}^{*}\approx-12.44433,

while (6,3.71875)(6,3.71875) is second-best with an estimated gap 0.089010.08901. As a Monte Carlo-error sensitivity check, we form two-sided Student-tt intervals for all 85 archived means using Bonferroni allocation 0.05/850.05/85. The simultaneous interval for fL∗f_{L}^{*} is [−12.46684,−12.42181][-12.46684,-12.42181], and its upper endpoint lies 0.054000.05400 below the smallest lower endpoint among the other 84 actions. A separate pointwise Welch interval for the runner-up gap is [0.07623,0.10179][0.07623,0.10179].

The heavy-tailed model also changes the coarse-grid geometry. The recovered nonpreemptive code uses (143). For K=(3,3,2)K=(3,3,2), an exhaustive audit against its 85 saved reference means gives family sizes 1,169,5291,169,529; all cases are nonautomatic. The uniform reference margins are 0.542513520.54251352, 0.867202110.86720211, and 0.433183650.43318365, reproducing the earlier rounded values 0.5430.543, 0.8670.867, and 0.4330.433. Propagating the simultaneous action intervals through the complete guardian-preserving families gives conservative lower margins 0.057530.05753, 0.734680.73468, and 0.369800.36980. Thus the reference ranking and all three guardian margins remain positive after accounting for the reported Monte Carlo standard errors under the usual replication-level tt-interval assumptions. The calculation does not control unknown transient bias or replace the missing historical metadata, so it is not a true-objective guardian certificate and we retain the term “reference.” Top-1 applied to these reference estimates discards the reference-optimal refinement path and ends at the reference second-best master-grid action. These statements concern estimated objective values and are not included in the finite-sample theorem.

The first moderate-horizon runs were visibly noisier than in the light-tailed benchmark. This is a descriptive comparison rather than an isolated service-tail effect: the objective geometry and retention vector also change. To distinguish a structural failure from a finite-horizon effect within this lognormal model, we then increased all stage targets proportionally. Table 8 shows a clear concentration pattern. At the largest well-replicated horizon, 49 of 50 runs select the reference master-grid optimizer; the pointwise 95% Wilson interval for the corresponding replication frequency is [0.8950,0.9965][0.8950,0.9965], conditional on treating the reference target as fixed. The first three rows use cumulative per-action stage targets (60,200,600,2000)(60,200,600,2000), (120,400,1200,4000)(120,400,1200,4000), and (240,800,2400,8000)(240,800,2400,8000), with 30, 30, and 16 replications and seed ranges 505000505000–505029505029, 510000510000–510029510029, and 520000520000–520015520015. The last two rows use targets (480,1600,4800,16000)(480,1600,4800,16000) and (960,3200,9600,32000)(960,3200,9600,32000), 50 replications each, and seeds 94000009400000–94000499400049 and 95000009500000–95000499500049. The saved 50-replication rows do not match the bundled driver’s request for 100 replications or its seed formulas. The provenance package therefore supplies a wrapper reconstructed from the saved rows and labels it as reconstructed, not as the historical generating driver. The uneven replication counts 30,30,16,50,5030,30,16,50,50 reflect successive experimental extensions and the archived outputs that remain available; they were not chosen to give equal precision or power across horizons.

A separate fixed-action diagnostic examines the queue-length tail at (s,p)=(5,3.9375)(s,p)=(5,3.9375). The retained simulator routine uses the continuous-time occupation estimator

p^r,n=1Tr∫0Tr𝟏{Qr(t)≥n}dt\widehat{p}_{r,n}=\frac{1}{T_{r}}\int_{0}^{T_{r}}\mathbf{1}\{Q_{r}(t)\geq n\}\,dt

The general theory in Section 4 does not require the primitive queueing state to be a CTMC; the selected-cycle route is formulated through polynomial moment and boundary-growth conditions. We do not, however, claim here that the strongest common-Lyapunov sufficient condition has been verified for the lognormal M/G/sM/G/s model. We therefore interpret this experiment as a numerical robustness test beyond the easiest analytically verifiable cases.

5.5 Comparison in a gradient-favorable regime

This final benchmark is intentionally unfavorable to a “one method fits all” interpretation. It asks how much is gained when a smooth model admits reliable, purpose-built queueing sensitivities. We close the substantive comparisons with the joint pricing–staffing M/M/1M/M/1 example of Chen, Liu, and Hong [1]. With the common demand function, holding-cost coefficient h0=1h_{0}=1, and staffing cost 0.1​μ20.1\mu^{2}, its objective is

f⁡(μ,p)=λ⁡(p)μ−λ⁡(p)+0.1​μ2−p​λ​(p).f(\mu,p)=\frac{\lambda(p)}{\mu-\lambda(p)}+0.1\mu^{2}-p\lambda(p).

On the comparison rectangle [6.7,12]×[3.7,7.5][6.7,12]\times[3.7,7.5], the exact optimum is approximately

(μ∗,p∗)=(7.10311,4.02337),f∗=−13.12610.(\mu^{*},p^{*})=(7.10311,4.02337),\qquad f^{*}=-13.12610.

GOLiQ starts at (12,7.5)(12,7.5) and uses the published schedules ηk=1/k\eta_{k}=1/k and Dk=⌈10+10​log⁡k⌉D_{k}=\lceil 10+10\log k\rceil, rounding the service-entry target up to an integer as in the archived source. For Top-KK, we use the hierarchy

3×3→5×5→9×9→17×17→33×333\times 3\to 5\times 5\to 9\times 9\to 17\times 17\to 33\times 33

with D=50D=50 and K=(1,2,4,4)K=(1,2,4,4). The recovered five-level source uses closed half-parent-mesh boxes, as in (141), but with the coordinate-specific meshes 5.3/(nℓ−1)5.3/(n_{\ell}-1) and 3.8/(nℓ−1)3.8/(n_{\ell}-1). The low, medium, and large comparisons use cumulative per-action cycle targets (4,8,14,20,26)(4,8,14,20,26), (10,20,35,50,65)(10,20,35,50,65), and (20,40,70,100,130)(20,40,70,100,130), respectively. An independent exhaustive audit reproduces its pruning-family sizes 1,4,26,66671,4,26,6667 and positive uniform margins approximately 4.873231374.87323137, 3.295084913.29508491, 1.155519541.15551954, and 0.230641490.23064149. One level-1 active set preserves a guardian automatically; the finite minimum there is taken over the other three sets. Rational interval bounds certify their positivity and the unique master-grid optimizer (7.03125,4.05625)(7.03125,4.05625). The implementation’s comparison tolerance preserves the intended closed-box child sets. This grid optimum has cost fL∗≈−13.12248055f_{L}^{*}\approx-13.12248055, giving the discretization gap fL∗−f∗≈0.00361515f_{L}^{*}-f^{*}\approx 0.00361515 in Table 2. It is the smallest terminal gap relative to the full-domain optimum attainable by a recommendation on this master grid.

This is a hierarchy certificate. In the recovered source, the direct-SAA cycle counts DD service entries and has cost

Gt=∫cycle ​tQ⁡(u)​𝑑u+0.1​μt2​Tt−pt​Jt,G_{t}=\int_{\text{cycle }t}Q(u)\,du+0.1\mu_{t}^{2}T_{t}-p_{t}J_{t},

where JtJ_{t} is the random number of external arrivals during the cycle, which need not equal DD. A service entry occurs at an arrival to an empty system or at a departure followed by immediate refill. The cycle ends after the DDth such entry; an inherited in-service customer and a capacity change are not counted as new entries. This continuous-time Markov chain uses total customer count QQ, rather than the workload integral of the first benchmark. It is distinct from the fixed-arrival workload construction of Proposition 4.4; the sampling and moment hypotheses for this implementation have not been verified by that proposition.

The archived GOLiQ comparator retains an already scheduled arrival and its stored price across a policy update, following [1, Section 3.3]; its updated price applies after that arrival. Direct Top-KK instead applies its new price immediately to subsequent arrivals. The two methods share a fixed-action objective but use different transient price-switching conventions. The numerical effect of that difference has not been isolated.

GOLiQ’s update uses completed waiting times observed at service entry and busy-period ages recorded at the corresponding arrivals, together with the known demand function and its derivative. The recovered code discards the first ⌊0.25​Dk⌋\lfloor 0.25D_{k}\rfloor customer observations from its gradient average. Customer-count and staffing integrals and realized revenue are recorded for evaluation, not supplied to that gradient. In particular, evaluation revenue is the sum of prices actually charged to arrivals, including the stored price of a pending arrival; all elapsed time and costs are counted despite gradient trimming. For pseudo-regret, the integrand in (140) uses the stationary objective at the current action label. It therefore does not reproduce the transient revenue effect of a pending arrival carrying its stored earlier price; that effect is included in realized cost.

Table 10 uses service-entry budgets matched exactly within every paired replication. Elapsed operating times remain random and are not matched. An audit of the archived driver found that its Python-level seed did not seed the Numba-compiled Top-KK simulator, so Top-KK inherited Numba state from the preceding GOLiQ run. The corrected driver seeds the Top-KK action order, Top-KK simulator, and GOLiQ explicitly and independently, then reruns all 300 pairs. In this gradient-favorable regime, GOLiQ uses smooth local sensitivity information very efficiently and achieves much smaller terminal gaps as well as lower mean pseudo-regret and realized-regret rates. The comparison therefore serves as a boundary-of-scope check: when reliable model-specific sensitivity structure is available, it can be substantially more efficient to exploit that structure than to replace it with direct ranking.

Table 11 reports both resource measures and the two learning-cost rates. The common service-entry count varies across pairs because the Top-KK final active set is random, but is identical for the two methods within each pair. Top-KK takes more elapsed time at the same entry count in these samples, so raw cumulative regret would combine policy loss with a different clock horizon. We therefore compare Rps​(H)/HR^{\mathrm{ps}}(H)/H and Rreal​(H)/HR^{\mathrm{real}}(H)/H, while displaying clock time explicitly. Parentheses for entries and time contain sample standard deviations; parentheses for the two rates contain Monte Carlo standard errors.

As a descriptive uncertainty check, the mean paired Top-KK minus GOLiQ pseudo-regret-rate differences are 3.2523.252, 3.5883.588, and 3.6683.668 at the low, medium, and large budgets. Their pointwise 95%95\% tt intervals are [3.130,3.374][3.130,3.374], [3.534,3.642][3.534,3.642], and [3.630,3.706][3.630,3.706], respectively. Thus the claim of lower GOLiQ pseudo-regret rate is supported by the retained samples. It remains specific to the event-matched design and does not assert equal-clock-time efficiency or a general algorithmic ordering.

5.6 Computational specification and provenance

Table 12 consolidates the experimental record. “Full” means that source or deterministic calculations, inputs, randomization, raw output, and aggregation are sufficient to reproduce or independently check the displayed object. “Partial” means that saved raw output is traceable but some historical driver, seed, or burn-in information is absent. “Archival” means that the recovered record is limited to a historical summary or figure and validation material. The accompanying machine-readable manifest gives filenames, exact seed ranges, stage targets, switching and tie rules, and the known gaps for each object; its validation script reaggregates the retained raw data and checks the manuscript figure hashes.

The classifications concern computational traceability, not theoretical verification. For example, the full canonical light-tailed record makes its reported summaries reproducible but does not by itself prove a general algorithmic ordering. Likewise, a full simulation record would not remove the reference-value uncertainty in the heavy-tailed model.

5.7 Summary of the numerical evidence

The experiments support a deliberately qualified conclusion. When the goal is accurate terminal identification from direct queue operation, Top-KK can be stronger than the corrected LiQUAR comparator in the reported exact-workload samples, although LiQUAR has lower median cumulative learning cost at the large budget. In the canonical mixed-integer staffing experiment, Top-KK has lower mean terminal gaps and higher optimizer-selection frequencies than Top-1 and flat SAA at each approximately clock-matched budget; all six reported independent mean-gap contrasts exclude zero. In the lognormal benchmark, rankings stabilize only at longer horizons and the identification effect remains visible. Because objective geometry and KK also change, this experiment does not isolate a causal service-tail effect. The final GOLiQ comparison also marks an important boundary: when smooth, reliable model-specific sensitivity information is available, a specialized gradient method can be much more efficient.

6 Discussion

Where direct Top-KK is most useful.

The numerical evidence argues against viewing direct SAA as a replacement for all queue-learning methods. Direct Top-KK is most attractive when objective observations are easy to accumulate but sensitivity formulas are inconvenient, when controls are discrete or mixed, or when the principal objective is high-quality terminal policy identification rather than minimum cumulative learning loss. The final GOLiQ comparison complements these cases by showing the value of exploiting a reliable model-specific gradient on a smooth problem.

Two roles of Top-KK.

The experiments reveal two distinct reasons to retain more than one parent. First, coarse-grid objective ranking can distort descendant quality: a guardian can be outranked even under exact objective values, as in the original M/M/1M/M/1 hierarchy, and under the estimated reference values in the heavy-tailed M/G/sM/G/s example. Second, even when exact-objective Top-1 would follow the correct path, finite-sample SAA noise can eliminate it; the mixed-staffing M/M/sM/M/s benchmark illustrates this statistical protection role. Proposition 4.3 distinguishes these mechanisms at a common active set, and the guardian theorem propagates retention through stages under its full-family separation condition. This does not establish dominance of Top-KK over Top-1 at a fixed total budget.

Transient effects and heavy tails.

The direct-SAA decomposition isolates accumulated conditional transient bias from martingale fluctuation. Contiguous action blocks are helpful because bias-function terms telescope internally, leaving only block boundaries. The lognormal experiment suggests that heavy-tailed service can make these finite horizons practically much more demanding: rare long services create long-lived congestion and slow stabilization of rankings. The long-horizon experiment shows that this need not prevent accurate identification, but it raises an important theoretical question about verifying weaker polynomial stability conditions without a common geometric-drift assumption. This interpretation is supported at the fixed diagnostic action by the exact-baseline comparison around level 20, although the archived exponential estimate at level 30 is too sparse for validation. The cross-benchmark interpretation remains suggestive because the objective geometry and retention vector are not held fixed.

Terminal identification versus cumulative regret.

The finite-sample and asymptotic theorems target the terminal recommendation, which is close to a simple-regret objective. Cumulative regret charges the exploration blocks themselves. In the corrected large-budget LiQUAR sensitivity study, shorter periods reduce median cumulative learning cost but increase the median terminal gap relative to the corrected baseline. This illustrates why the two objectives need to be reported separately. A cumulative regret analysis for blocked CTF is therefore a useful extension rather than an implicit consequence of the present identification theory.

Scalability and limitations.

A finite hierarchy makes integer and categorical controls natural and avoids a projection or nonlinear solver at each update, but the number of candidate actions can still grow rapidly with dimension. Top-KK reduces the number of actions sampled deeply, yet high-dimensional problems may require sparse coordinate refinement, problem-specific hierarchies, or local borrowing across nearby actions. Guardian separation is also a genuine structural condition: if every parent leading to a master-grid optimizer is ranked below KℓK_{\ell} competing regions even under the true objective, additional sampling cannot repair deterministic mis-refinement.

Tuning and verification still needed.

A practical data-driven retention rule would need to balance the risk of discarding an optimal region against the cost of sampling its descendants. The present fixed-KK analysis identifies this tradeoff but does not solve it. Full guardian-family audits are now available for the exact-formula hierarchies documented above. The light-tailed staffing comparison now has a canonical shared driver and a fully retained simulation record; that computational validation remains distinct from a theorem establishing equal-resource or universal superiority. The exhaustive lognormal reference audit now includes simultaneous Monte Carlo-error sensitivity bounds, but missing transient-bias and historical run metadata still preclude a certificate for true-objective margins. Proposition 4.4 completes the common Lyapunov and weighted cycle-reward verification for the specified M/M/1M/M/1 workload model. Extending that verification to other queueing models remains substantive work; the duration bound alone is not a stability argument. These distinctions separate the conditional theorems, the current numerical evidence, and the remaining validation tasks.

Further directions.

Several extensions are natural. The master grid may be refined with the total budget if estimation errors vanish relative to shrinking guardian margins. Quantitative guarantees under delayed or imperfect cost observation require control of the accumulated observation error at the actual ranking times; Remark 4.11 gives the corresponding transfer bound. Heavy-tailed models motivate direct verification of selected-cycle polynomial moment conditions. Finally, in large service systems it would be useful to compare direct learned integer staffing with square-root staffing prescriptions in the Halfin–Whitt regime, thereby quantifying when online learning adds value over classical asymptotic rules.

7 Conclusion

This paper develops a direct sample-average route to queueing control on a single persistent operating trajectory. Fixed-event-count cycles provide the cost-rate estimator; the transient-bias/martingale decomposition explains its error; and regenerative boundary representations show why contiguous action blocks can control inherited-state effects without resetting the queue.

Top-KK coarse-to-fine search turns that estimator into a structured decision procedure. Guardian retention connects finite-stage ranking accuracy to master-grid identification and distinguishes two reasons to retain multiple parents: deterministic coarse-grid distortion and finite-sample mis-ranking. The exact-objective Top-1 failure in the four-level M/M/1M/M/1 hierarchy gives a concrete structural example of the first mechanism. For the specified persistent-workload M/M/1M/M/1 implementation, the paper verifies the common drift, bias representation, cycle-reward moments, duration control, and completed-stage sampling assumptions needed by the theory. Other queueing models require their own verification.

The numerical results separate terminal identification from the operating cost of learning. Top-KK has a terminal-gap advantage in the reported exact-workload LiQUAR comparison, whereas corrected LiQUAR has lower median cumulative learning cost at the large budget. The canonical mixed-integer staffing experiment shows lower mean terminal gaps and higher optimizer-selection frequencies for Top-KK than for Top-1 and flat SAA across three approximately clock-matched budgets, illustrating the value of protecting several refinement paths in this design. The lognormal-service experiment shows slower finite-horizon stabilization and is interpreted as a robustness test rather than a completed heavy-tail verification. The GOLiQ comparison marks the opposite boundary: a specialized gradient method can be much more efficient when reliable model-specific sensitivities are available.

Accordingly, the contribution is not a universal replacement for gradient or bandit methods. It is a complementary framework for problems in which realized objective costs are observable, the queue persists across control changes, and the operational decision space makes direct ranking and structured refinement more credible than a model-specific gradient construction.
